note: Rows of the A² Values Library linked to each book (key = book number). "used in Book NN" = the book's own value; "close to Book NN" = the same value in other traditions. Use the source and reliability note when citing; respect care_flag. Religious traditions (hadith, gospels, Kabbalah, Buddhist texts) are left out on purpose: the series and its articles stay secular.

2.meaning_for_kids: Some good things cannot be rushed; we wait until everyone and everything is ready.
2.saying: We wait for the right time for our ceremonies and our meetings.
2.source: Miriam-Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann, essay 'Dadirri' (Ngangikurungkurr, Daly River region NT), as hosted by the Uniting Church in Australia (eden.uca.org.au); also Miriam-Rose Foundation, 'Dadirri' (miriamrosefoundation.org.au/dadirri).
2.reliability: Sentence as read in the essay text; the context is the community’s own timing of meetings and ceremonies. Only the idea of waiting is used here, never the ceremonies.

2.culture_region: Quechua weavers, Chinchero and Cusco region (Peru)
2.meaning_for_kids: Big, beautiful things are made slowly, one row at a time, often learned from grandma.
2.saying: Girls learn to weave from mothers and grandmothers, and each community's designs carry its history. "Each interlacing thread is a recording of movement, tension, and emotion… Each tells a story."
2.source: Smithsonian Folklife Magazine, 'The Guiding Thread' (Chinchero weavers); Center for Traditional Textiles of Cusco (founded 1996, directed by Nilda Callañaupa Alvarez)
2.reliability: Living craft documented by the Smithsonian and the CTTC

2.value: Staying calm and quiet while you wait
2.meaning_for_kids: Patient people stay calm, wait quietly, and don't make a fuss when things take time.
2.saying: "Three things that characterise every patient person: repose, silence, blushing."
2.original: Trí thúarascbait cach n-ainmnetach: sámtha, túa, imderead.
2.source: The Triads of Ireland, ed. & tr. Kuno Meyer (Todd Lecture Series XIII, 1906), §189
2.reliability: Old Irish text, c. 850-900 CE; Meyer's translation (public domain)

2.value: Time will tell: wait and see
2.meaning_for_kids: We don't always know right away how things will turn out; waiting helps us find out.
2.saying: Time is a good storyteller (meaning "time will tell").
2.original: Is maith an scéalaí an aimsir.
2.source: Irish proverb (seanfhocal): Ó Dónaill, Foclóir Gaeilge–Béarla (1977), on teanglann.ie, s.v. aimsir, sense 2 'Time' (gloss 'time will tell'); also on gleg.ie/gaeilge/seanfhocail/
2.reliability: Widely recorded Irish proverb; headword entry in Ó Dónaill. The literal English is accurate; the dictionary gloss is 'time will tell'.

2.value: Let things grow in their own time
2.meaning_for_kids: Seeds, wobbly teeth and new skills need time; pulling or rushing only spoils them.
2.saying: A farmer of Song, worried his sprouts were not growing fast enough, tugged each one up a little and came home proud: 'I helped them grow!' By morning they had withered.
2.original: 宋人有閔其苗之不長而揠之者。
2.source: Mencius 2A2 (Gongsun Chou I); idiom 揠苗助長
2.reliability: Canonical Mencius parable; idiom in everyday use

2.culture_region: Ancient Greece and Rome; Aesopic fables
2.value: Little by little, with a clever plan
2.meaning_for_kids: When something is hard, think of a plan and do it one small step at a time.
2.saying: A thirsty crow drops pebble after pebble into a pitcher until the water rises high enough to drink. “Little by little does the trick.”
2.source: Aesop, The Crow and the Pitcher (Perry Index 390; Avianus; Bianor); moral as worded by J. Jacobs (1894)
2.reliability: Ancient fable (Perry 390); Pliny the Elder links it to real crow behaviour, confirmed in modern corvid studies

2.value: Bearing hard times patiently and calmly
2.meaning_for_kids: When we must wait or something is hard, we stay calm and keep going.
2.saying: Gaman: "enduring the seemingly unbearable with patience and dignity."
2.source: Japanese cultural value; described as rooted in Zen Buddhist teaching

2.value: Stay with it, even when it is hard
2.meaning_for_kids: New things can feel cold and hard at first, but if you keep trying patiently, they warm up.
2.saying: Even a cold stone grows warm if you sit on it for three years.
2.original: 石の上にも三年 (ishi no ue ni mo san nen)
2.source: Japanese proverb (kotowaza); Digital Daijisen, Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (first example Saikaku, Saikaku oridome, 1694) and Kotowaza o shiru jiten, via Kotobank
2.reliability: Widely recorded proverb; the early form was 'sit three years on a stone and it warms'; 'three years' means a good long while, not a literal count

2.meaning_for_kids: Some good things need time, like fruit ripening, so we wait instead of grabbing too soon.
2.saying: Don't pick things now; they will bear fruit later.
2.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian school tablets (c. 1800 BCE)

2.meaning_for_kids: Waiting calmly and not giving up, even when something takes a long time.
2.saying: "Ahonui", meaning patience, to be expressed with perseverance.
2.reliability: Official statute text; a modern legal codification of Native Hawaiian values

2.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
2.meaning_for_kids: If you wait calmly and keep going, even hard, slow things turn out well in the end.
2.saying: He who is patient can cook a stone and enjoy its broth.
2.original: Mai haƙuri shi yakan dafa dutse ya sha romonsa.
2.source: Hausa proverb, Yusuf Sadau Saleh, 'A Contrastive Analysis of English and Hausa Proverbs in Selected Texts', M.Ed. thesis, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, 2014, p. 32 (patience)
2.reliability: Hausa text and English gloss printed in a university thesis (page number inferred from the extracted text); the saying is widely repeated in Hausa proverb sources. English is the thesis's wording, lightly edited.

2.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
2.culture_region: Fulani / Fulɓe (Sahel, from Senegal to Nigeria)
2.meaning_for_kids: Stay calm and keep your feelings in check when things are hard or you have to wait.
2.saying: Munyal (patience, endurance, self-control) is one of the core tenets of pulaaku, the Fulani code of conduct, alongside modesty (semteende) and care and forethought (hakkiilo).
2.source: Pulaaku, the Fulɓe code of conduct: Adamu Shede, 'Fulɓe Code of Conduct (Pulaaku) as Portrayed in Their Proverbs', M.A. thesis, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, 2014 (abstract; the thesis cites Stenning's gloss of munyal as 'endurance'); New World Encyclopedia, 'Fulani' (munyal: 'patience, self control, discipline, prudence')
2.reliability: WEAKER: concept named in a university thesis abstract and a general encyclopedia; I did not see the thesis's proverb chapter, so no Fulfulde proverb is attached. Pulaaku is described as a code used to teach young people etiquette; the Fulɓe are mostly Muslim, but the code is presented as a cultural one.

16.value: Caring for Country is a family duty
16.meaning_for_kids: Looking after the land and its animals is a job families share and hand down to their children.
16.saying: “Caring for the land and its wildlife is fundamental to Aboriginal people’s culture.” Cultural responsibilities are “passed from one generation to the next”.
16.source: Parks Australia / Australian Government (DCCEEW), Kakadu National Park, 'The traditional owners – Bininj/Mungguy'.
16.reliability: Government visitor page about the Bininj/Mungguy Traditional Owners; Kakadu is jointly managed with Traditional Owners. The same page covers Creation ancestors, ceremony and kinship skin groups, which are deliberately not used.

16.value: The Earth is our mother; care for her
16.meaning_for_kids: The earth feeds and shelters us, so we look after it like family.
16.saying: "Celebrating nature, the Pacha Mama (Mother Earth), of which we are a part…"
16.source: Constitution of Ecuador (2008), Preamble; Andean Quechua & Aymara tradition
16.reliability: Official constitutional wording; Pachamama is also a sacred figure in living Andean spirituality

16.value: Not blocking the water others need
16.meaning_for_kids: Water and nature are for everyone (plants, animals and neighbours), so don't block or waste them.
16.saying: 'I have never stopped the flow of water of a neighbor.' (one of the declarations of innocence)
16.source: Book of the Dead, spell 125 'declarations of innocence' (Papyrus of Ani, BM EA 10470); trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1898)
16.reliability: Primary funerary text; wording of the declarations varies from papyrus to papyrus

16.value: Living side by side with nature
16.meaning_for_kids: We use the woods and fields gently, so plants and animals can keep living there too.
16.saying: Satoyama is the border zone between mountain foothills and farmland, where villagers' careful cutting and leaf-gathering over centuries kept woods healthy and full of species.
16.source: Japanese traditional village landscape and land management (Edo period onward)

16.value: Guarding and caring for our world
16.meaning_for_kids: Looking after the places, plants and animals around you like a guardian.
16.saying: Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.
16.source: Te Ara – Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Kaitiakitanga – guardianship and conservation'; Te Aka Māori Dictionary, s.v. kaitiakitanga ('guardianship, stewardship, trusteeship'); NZQA Ngā Matapono ('guardianship and preservation')
16.reliability: Encyclopedia of New Zealand text; consistent with Te Aka and NZQA. Core Māori value; already the subject of Book 16.

16.value: When land and sea thrive, we thrive
16.meaning_for_kids: Looking after the land and water is how we all stay healthy and fed.
16.saying: If the land is well and the sea is well, the people will thrive.
16.original: Toitū te marae a Tāne, toitū te marae a Tangaroa, toitū te iwi
16.source: Te Papa, 'Ko au te taiao' teaching resource, 'What does a better world look like?' (wording and translation)
16.reliability: Wording and translation from Te Papa. Its final phrase is also quoted elsewhere as 'toitū te tangata' (variant not opened). The saying names two atua as domains of land and sea, so keep story_seed secular and consult knowledge keepers.

16.value: Caring for the little bees at home
16.meaning_for_kids: Even tiny creatures like bees need gentle care, and they help the plants and people around them.
16.saying: Yucatec Maya families keep stingless bees (xúnan káab) in hollowed-log hives called jobon in the family yard, treating them as companions linked to the forest and the milpa.
16.source: Veronica Briseño Castrejón (Univ. of Calgary), 'Unveiling Meliponiculture: Decolonizing Maya Stingless Beekeeping in the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico', Eva Crane Trust, summarising her 2024 doctoral fieldwork
16.reliability: Researcher's summary of fieldwork on a living practice (bee name also given as Ko'olel káab; Melipona beecheii). Hive ceremonies are described there but deliberately not used in the story

16.value: Caring for a baby animal in need
16.meaning_for_kids: When we gently feed and care for a small creature, it feels safe and its family trusts us.
16.saying: Finding the giant Anzud bird's chick alone, Lugalbanda feeds it honey cakes and meat and tidies its nest; the delighted parent bird rewards him with tireless speed.
16.source: Lugalbanda and the Anzud bird (ETCSL 1.8.2.2), ll. 50-183
16.reliability: Primary text; Sumerian epic, ETCSL (Oxford) translation; Lugalbanda's care is partly meant to win the bird's favour

16.value: Thinking of those not yet born
16.meaning_for_kids: Before you choose, think how it will help the children who come long after you.
16.saying: The Seventh Generation is a core Haudenosaunee value: decisions take 'into consideration those who are not yet born but who will inherit the world.'
16.source: Haudenosaunee Confederacy, 'Values' page (haudenosauneeconfederacy.com/values): 'a core value called the Seventh Generation'.
16.reliability: Published by the Haudenosaunee Confederacy itself; core principle of Haudenosaunee governance.

16.meaning_for_kids: Pick, catch or use only what your family needs, so there is plenty left for later.
16.saying: Using nature's bounty for the well-being of person and community without jeopardising 'the integrity, diversity, or productivity of our environment', 'only taking what you, your family, and/or your community may need.'
16.source: Unama'ki Institute of Natural Resources (UINR), 'Netukulimk' (uinr.ca); Nova Scotia curriculum resource 'Netukulimk' (Oct 2020, citing Kerry Prosper, Albert Marshall, Murdena Marshall and other Elders).
16.reliability: Defined by a Mi'kmaw natural-resources organisation and a Nova Scotia government curriculum resource; also a Mi'kmaw rights/law concept.

16.value: Keeping water, earth and fire clean
16.meaning_for_kids: We never dirty rivers, soil or air, because every living thing needs them clean.
16.saying: The Avesta and other Zoroastrian texts call for the protection of water, earth, fire and air; pollution of the good creation is to be avoided.
16.source: Avesta, Vendidad (sanctity of fire, earth and water: Fargards 3, 6, 8); Zoroastrian purity laws

16.value: Caring for the land that feeds us
16.meaning_for_kids: Looking after plants, water and animals, because the land takes care of us too.
16.saying: "He aliʻi ka ʻāina; he kauwā ke kanaka." The land is a chief; man is its servant. (ʻŌlelo Noʻeau 531)
16.original: He aliʻi ka ʻāina; he kauwā ke kanaka
16.source: Pukui, ʻŌlelo Noʻeau (1983), no. 531; value 'Mālama ʻĀina – care for the land' in UH College of Education, Growing Pono Schools cards
16.reliability: Recorded proverb (Pukui 1983, #531); number confirmed by a University of Hawaiʻi resource

16.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
16.culture_region: Mande / Malinke (Mali, Guinea); Manden Charter, c. 1236
16.value: Look up before you light a fire
16.meaning_for_kids: Before you do something big, look all around, even up high, so you don't hurt creatures you can't see.
16.saying: Before setting fire to the bush, don't look down at the ground, raise your head in the direction of the top of the trees.
16.source: Manden Charter (Kouroukan Fouga), Article 38, English text translated from French, 'Kouroukan Fouga - Indigenous Constitution of Ancient Mali' (ccaf.africa); the Charter is inscribed by UNESCO as 'the Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga' (2009, decision 4.COM 13.59)
16.reliability: Oral charter attributed to c. 1236; a French version was published in 1998 and this English text is a translation from French, so wording and numbering vary slightly between versions. UNESCO calls it one of the oldest constitutions in the world, albeit mainly oral. The Charter gives the rule without a reason; reading it as protecting what lives in the treetops (fruit, flowers, nests) is an interpretation.

18.culture_region: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander (Firesticks Alliance, national network)
18.value: Care for Country and it cares for you
18.meaning_for_kids: Look after the place that feeds and shelters you, and it will look after you too.
18.saying: Firesticks Alliance works from the belief that when you properly care for Country, Country will care for you.
18.source: Firesticks Alliance Indigenous Corporation case study, NSW Department of Planning (Oct 2023).
18.reliability: Aboriginal-led organisation’s guiding belief as stated in a NSW Government case study; the idea is widely stated by First Nations land-care groups. Wording rendered plainly from page text: check the PDF before quoting in print.

18.value: Giving and receiving help in turn
18.meaning_for_kids: When a friend helps you, you help them back, so everyone is cared for.
18.saying: Ayni is mutual help: neighbours work each other's fields or houses and the help is returned in turn, "a core value that has served generations of Andean people since pre-Inka times."
18.source: Smithsonian NMAI, Native Knowledge 360°, 'Reciprocity—Andean Style' (Inka water unit); B. Mannheim, 'The Language of Reciprocity in Southern Peruvian Quechua', Anthropological Linguistics (1986)
18.reliability: Well-documented living practice (museum and ethnographic sources)

18.culture_region: Quechua communities, Cusco region (Peru); wider Andes
18.value: Giving back to the earth that gives
18.meaning_for_kids: When nature gives us food, we say thank you and give something back, like planting and caring.
18.saying: Quechua communities see a "reciprocal relationship with the land, each other"; the Earth's gifts "must be reciprocated through the giving of pagos, or offerings."
18.source: Heinrich Böll Foundation, 'The Potato Park of Peru' (2016); Smithsonian NMAI, 'Reciprocity—Andean Style' (offering after trail work on the Qhapaq Ñan)
18.reliability: Living ritual practice described by reputable foundation and museum sources; ritual details are sacred and should not be depicted

18.meaning_for_kids: We help our neighbours with big jobs, and they help us when it's our turn.
18.saying: The meitheal is the Irish "co-operative labour system" in which "groups of neighbours help each other in turn with farming work such as harvesting crops."
18.source: Irish rural custom of the meitheal (work party), as described in Wikipedia 'Meitheal'
18.reliability: Well-documented Irish rural custom, still used for community volunteering

18.meaning_for_kids: Be kind to little ones; one day the smallest friend may be the one who helps you.
18.saying: A lion spares a mouse who pleads, 'If you spare me... I shall make you escape from your misfortune.' Later the mouse gnaws through the straps that bind the lion.
18.source: 'The Lion in Search of Man', fable in the Demotic Myth of the Eye of the Sun (Leiden Demotic Papyrus I 384, 17/9-18/34); Lichtheim, AEL III (1980), pp. 156-159
18.reliability: Primary text, 2nd-century CE Demotic papyrus; a shorter version is known from Aesop

18.value: All living things help one another
18.meaning_for_kids: Bees help flowers, flowers feed bees: we all need each other, so we help each other.
18.saying: Souls render service to one another.
18.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21 (Jain motto on the Jain emblem)
18.reliability: Canonical Jain sutra; motto on the Jain emblem adopted by all sects

18.meaning_for_kids: Help a friend with their job today, and they'll help you with yours tomorrow.
18.saying: Pumasi is the traditional village custom of exchanging labour: neighbours work together on one household's field or kimchi-making, then the next, helping each in turn.
18.source: Traditional Korean labour-exchange custom; as described in Wikipedia 'Pumasi' (citing Korea Times, 2013)
18.reliability: Well-documented farming custom, still seen in communal kimchi-making

18.meaning_for_kids: When everyone adds a little, there is enough for all.
18.saying: With your food basket and my food basket, the people will thrive.
18.original: Nāu te rourou, nāku te rourou, ka ora ai te iwi
18.source: Tāhūrangi (Ministry of Education), Akona te Tau, 'Summer Food – Kānga' (wording; rourou explained as a flax food basket and symbol of giving and sharing, linked to manaakitanga); English gloss ('With my food basket and your food basket the people will prosper') from the Playcentre Aotearoa whakataukī sheet
18.reliability: Wording confirmed on a Ministry of Education resource, which gives no English; the English gloss is from Playcentre. Word order of the first two clauses varies between sources.

18.culture_region: Guatemala; Maya (Achí and other Maya peoples)
18.value: Good life for everyone, shared with the land
18.meaning_for_kids: Take only what you need and look after what everyone shares, so there is enough for all.
18.saying: Utz K'aslemal, the 'good life': well-being for all through a balanced relationship with nature, using what is needed without exhausting it, giving back, and guarding shared resources together.
18.source: Alfredo Itzep Manuel, 'Prácticas comunitarias y construcción del Buen Vivir en Guatemala: Experiencias desde el tejido social local en Qachuu Aloom', Ciencias Sociales y Humanidades (Univ. de San Carlos de Guatemala) vol. 12 no. 1 (2025), pp. 117-118
18.reliability: Peer-reviewed case report from a Guatemalan university; the term appears as Ut'z K'aslem'al (Achí) and Utz K'aslemal (Consejo del Pueblo Maya). Summary is paraphrased; a contemporary buen-vivir articulation, not a quoted ancient text

18.value: Kindness passes from hand to hand
18.meaning_for_kids: When someone shares with us we share back, and kindness keeps passing around.
18.saying: A hand will stretch out towards an outstretched hand. A hand will open for an opened hand.
18.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian school tablets (c. 1800 BCE)

18.value: Giving and giving back builds friendship
18.meaning_for_kids: Friends stay close when they share gifts and kindness back and forth.
18.saying: "Gift-givers' friendships are longest found, / If fair their fates may be" (st. 41); "And gifts with gifts requite" (st. 42).
18.original: viðrgefendr ok endrgefendr erusk lengst vinir, ef þat bíðr at verða vel (st. 41); Vin sínum skal maðr vinr vera ok gjalda gjöf við gjöf (st. 42)
18.source: Hávamál st. 41-42 (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1936 revised ed., text as on sacred-texts.com), stanza numbering per Bellows; same number in the Old Norse edition (Neckel / Guðni Jónsson)
18.reliability: Hávamál is in Codex Regius (c. 1270; poem older). Stanza number and Old Norse checked on heimskringla.no/wiki/Hávamál (Guðni Jónsson ed.); English checked word for word against Bellows on sacred-texts.com; quoted verbatim (earlier draft's 'who give and give again' is not in Bellows; replaced). Bellows st. 41 also opens 'Friends shall gladden each other with arms and garments'.

18.meaning_for_kids: In a family we notice each other and help each other, and we get help back.
18.saying: "Recognize others, be recognized; help others, be helped; such is a family relationship."
18.original: ʻIke aku, ʻike mai, kōkua aku, kōkua mai; pēlā iho lā ka nohana ʻohana
18.source: Pukui, ʻŌlelo Noʻeau (1983) (entry number not confirmed online); listed in University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo proverbs collection
18.reliability: Widely recorded ʻŌlelo Noʻeau on ʻohana; Pukui entry number not confirmed – check the book

18.meaning_for_kids: When I help you and you help me, we both end up better off.
18.saying: Hands wash each other: each hand cleans the other, so people who help one another both gain.
18.source: isiZulu proverb, Boston University African Language Program, African Proverbs Project, 'isiZulu Proverbs' (lesson 6); Setswana form in Gareegope, 'Aspect of Botho/Ubuntu in Botswana', University of Botswana Law Journal (June & Dec 2020), fn 40, p. 46
18.reliability: Widely recorded proverb in several Southern African languages

18.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
18.value: Help me and let me help you
18.meaning_for_kids: We all need help sometimes and can give help sometimes, so lend a hand and ask for one.
18.saying: 'Help me and let me help you': a symbol of cooperation and interdependence. A companion saying: the left hand washes the right and the right washes the left.
18.original: Boa me na me mmoa wo
18.source: Adinkra symbol Boa me na me mmoa wo, adinkrasymbols.org/symbols/boa-me-na-me-mmoa-wo/ (companion saying 'Benkum dware nifa na nifa nso adware benkum'); also MOMAA 'Adinkra Symbols: The Visual Language of West Africa' and CSDT (Culturally Situated Design Tools) 'Adinkra Symbols and Meanings' list, csdt.org ('Cooperation, interdependence')
18.reliability: Three published glossaries agree on the wording and meaning. Adinkra meanings are modern glosses compiled from tradition.
18.used_in_series: close to Book 18 (giving and receiving, asking for help)

10.culture_region: Yolngu (Crocodile Islands, Arnhem Land, Northern Territory)
10.value: Sharing your catch so everyone gets fed
10.meaning_for_kids: If you have more than you need, share it, especially with people who can’t get their own.
10.saying: “If you get more than you need for your family, you should share.” “Sharing is important because it means that people who can’t go out themselves can still get a feed.”
10.source: AIATSIS with the Crocodile Islands Rangers, 'Yolngu Fishing Values of the Crocodile Islands: Community Report for the Livelihood Values of Indigenous Customary Fishing Project' (Feb 2018), 'Rom and Cultural Values' p. 8 and 'Social Values' p. 9.
10.reliability: Community report from Yolngu interviews, prepared with the Crocodile Islands Rangers; sentences verbatim from the report text. Speaks for this community, not for all Aboriginal peoples.

10.value: Generosity to guests and anyone in need
10.meaning_for_kids: Share what you have gladly, especially with a visitor or someone who needs it.
10.saying: Hatim al-Tai (d. 578 CE), a chief and poet of Tayy, gave away nearly everything he owned; Arabs still say 'more generous than Hatim.'
10.source: Classical proverb 'akram min Hatim'; Hatim's lore in classical Arabic sources (e.g. Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-'Iqd al-Farid)
10.reliability: Widely recorded classical proverb; Hatim was historical, his stories are legendary embellishments

10.meaning_for_kids: Instead of always asking for things, we look for chances to give and share.
10.saying: Cormac on his youth: "I was gentle in friendship... I would not ask, but I would give."
10.source: Tecosca Cormaic (The Instructions of King Cormac mac Airt), tr. Kuno Meyer (Todd Lecture Series XV, 1909), §7
10.reliability: Old Irish gnomic text, c. 9th century, attributed to the legendary king Cormac; Meyer's translation (public domain)

10.value: Letting others have the bigger share
10.meaning_for_kids: When sharing treats, sometimes offer the bigger piece to someone else and feel proud.
10.saying: At four years old, Kong Rong let his brothers have the bigger pears and took a small one; the Three Character Classic still teaches: 'Rong, at four, could yield the pears.'
10.source: Three Character Classic (Song-dynasty primer); anecdote earlier in Li Xian's (Tang) commentary to the Book of the Later Han, Biography of Kong Rong, citing his family biography
10.reliability: Anecdote about a real Han figure; Three Character Classic line well attested; the Hou Hanshu-commentary origin was not checked online (double-check)

10.culture_region: Britain & United States; Masonic fraternity (18th-19th c.)
10.meaning_for_kids: Giving love and help freely is the greatest thing we can do, and it lasts.
10.saying: Of faith, hope and charity, charity is greatest, "for our faith may be lost in sight; hope ends in fruition; but charity extends beyond the grave."
10.source: Daniel Sickels, General Ahiman Rezon (1868), 'The Covering of the Lodge', pp. 79-80; cf. Webb: 'charity to all mankind'; 1 Corinthians 13:13
10.reliability: Published monitorial text (public domain); wording varies by jurisdiction

10.meaning_for_kids: If you have something good, share some of it with others.
10.source: Delphic maxims, Sosiades' list in Stobaeus, Anthology (Wachsmuth–Hense vol. 3, pp. 125–128), no. 45
10.reliability: Sosiades' list preserved by Stobaeus (5th c. AD); many maxims match a 4th–3rd c. BC stele from Miletopolis; Delphic origin is traditional

10.value: Giving even when you have little
10.meaning_for_kids: Even if we don't have much, we can share what we have with someone who needs it.
10.saying: A poor old man can't sell his straw hats in a blizzard, so he ties them on snow-covered roadside statues, and his own towel on the last; gifts arrive that night.
10.source: Japanese folktale (mukashibanashi); oldest recorded versions from Hokuriku
10.reliability: Traditional folktale with many regional variants; Buddhist setting (Jizō statues)

10.meaning_for_kids: Sharing your food, toys and time, especially with someone who has less.
10.saying: Core Lakota values are wówačhaŋtognaka (generosity), wówačhiŋtȟaŋka (perseverance), wóohitike (bravery) and wóksape (wisdom), which 'are exemplified in leadership.'
10.source: Lakota virtues: WoLakota Project, 'Lakota Virtues' (South Dakota Office of Indian Education; teachings shared by Lakota Elders); Crazy Horse School, Wanblee (Oglala Sioux Tribe), mission/values page; M. Van Heuvelen (Cheyenne River Sioux), 'Lakota Values Endure', NMAI Smithsonian Voices (2020).
10.reliability: Lakota virtue published by Lakota educators, a tribal school and the SD Office of Indian Education; spellings vary (wówačhaŋtognaka, Wacantognaka).

10.meaning_for_kids: Even when you only have a little, you share it with your family and friends.
10.saying: Children of the same descent share the head of a locust.
10.original: Vhana vha muthu vha kovhana ṱhoho ya nzie
10.source: Tshivenḓa proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 6
10.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal

10.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
10.meaning_for_kids: When someone visits, we greet them warmly, offer water, and share our food from the same bowl.
10.saying: Teranga, the Wolof ideal of hospitality, brings respect, community and sharing: a visitor is greeted 'may peace greet you here', offered water and a cola nut, and eats from the communal bowl.
10.source: Omar Marone, 'Teranga Among the Wolof People', Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife 1990 program book (adapted from Marone, Bulletin de l'IFAN 31B(3), 1969); definition also on Goshen College's Senegal Study-Service Term page ('hospitality ... respect, community and sharing')
10.reliability: Ethnographic essay by a professor at Cheikh Anta Diop University (Dakar), published by the Smithsonian; teranga is also Senegal's best-known national value. Practices vary by household and region.

17.culture_region: Yolngu (Crocodile Islands, Arnhem Land, Northern Territory)
17.value: Passing stories and knowledge to children
17.meaning_for_kids: Grown-ups and Elders tell you the stories and show you the ways so you can carry them on.
17.saying: Yolngu in the Crocodile Islands said that making sure knowledge and stories are passed down to the djamarrkuli (children) is a priority.
17.source: AIATSIS with the Crocodile Islands Rangers, 'Yolngu Fishing Values of the Crocodile Islands: Community Report for the Livelihood Values of Indigenous Customary Fishing Project' (Feb 2018), 'Rom and Cultural Values' p. 9.
17.reliability: Paraphrase of a sentence in the community report (“Making sure the knowledge and stories are passed down to the djamarrkuli…”); the report text was read in extraction and the sentence was cut short there.
17.used_in_series: close to Book 17 (wisdom of the past)

17.culture_region: Torres Strait Islander (Iama, Torres Strait, Queensland)
17.value: Learning island plants and animals from Elders
17.meaning_for_kids: Elders show young people the plants and animals around them, so they know and look after their home.
17.saying: TSRA Rangers report “facilitating the transfer of knowledge from Elders to young people about the plants and animals on Iama”.
17.source: Torres Strait Regional Authority, Land and Sea Management Unit, 'Ranger Achievements 2018'.
17.reliability: TSRA achievements booklet; sentence verbatim from the PDF text. It describes a ranger-program activity rather than a stated value, so the value is an inference. Weaker row.
17.used_in_series: close to Book 17 (wisdom of the past)

17.value: Learning from what we have already seen
17.meaning_for_kids: What already happened is 'in front' where we can see it, so we learn from it.
17.saying: In Aymara, nayra ('eye', 'front') also means the past and qhipa ('back') means the future: the known past lies before your eyes, the unknown future behind.
17.source: R. Núñez & E. Sweetser, 'With the Future Behind Them', Cognitive Science 30 (2006)
17.reliability: Peer-reviewed linguistic study; its explanation is partly debated
17.used_in_series: close to Book 17 (Wisdom of the past)

17.culture_region: Quechua (Andes); taught in Chile's Indigenous-language programme
17.meaning_for_kids: Grandparents and older people know many things; when we listen, we learn.
17.saying: Uyarispa yachaqayku: "We learn by listening." Kuraqkunata ñuqayku uyariyku: "We listen to our elders."
17.source: Chile, Ministry of Education (curriculumnacional.cl), Quechua language and culture programme, 2nd grade, Unit 3, suggested activity
17.reliability: Modern school-curriculum phrases expressing a traditional value; not an ancient proverb
17.used_in_series: close to Book 17 (Wisdom of the past)

17.meaning_for_kids: Old stories from grandparents hold useful lessons, so we listen and pass them on.
17.saying: The seanchaí was "a traditional Gaelic storyteller or historian"; "a large corpus of tales was passed from one practitioner to another without ever being written down."
17.source: Gaelic storytelling tradition of the seanchaí, as described in Wikipedia 'Seanchaí'
17.used_in_series: close to Book 17 (wisdom of the past)

17.value: Young ones grow strong leaning on elders
17.meaning_for_kids: Grandparents and older friends know a lot; listening to them helps you grow strong.
17.saying: A new bush is supported by the old one: the young who heed elders' counsel avoid needless mistakes.
17.original: Ṱanzu ḽiswa ḽi ima nga ḽilala
17.source: Tshivenḓa proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 12
17.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal
17.used_in_series: close to Book 17 (wisdom of the past)

13.meaning_for_kids: When someone new arrives, make them welcome and show them they are safe and wanted.
13.saying: “A Welcome to Country is performed by Aboriginal people to welcome visitors to their traditional lands.” Visitors once sought permission to enter, and hosts offered “safe passage”.
13.source: Government of Western Australia, Department of Education, guidance on Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country (education.wa.edu.au/dl/z69q2xg).
13.reliability: Education-department description of a protocol performed by Elders or Traditional Custodians. The first sentence is verbatim from the page text; the rest is summarised. Practice varies by nation, and schools should invite local people rather than perform it themselves.
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (belonging, door open to all)

13.value: Our community is one big family
13.meaning_for_kids: Your neighbours and friends are like family: everyone belongs and everyone looks out for each other.
13.saying: The ayllu is "the basic social unit in modern Andean society", a community of extended families in one area; under the Inca, plots were redistributed yearly so every family's needs were met.
13.source: G. F. McEwan, 'Ayllu', Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (via Encyclopedia.com)
13.reliability: Encyclopedic; well-documented social institution still active today

13.culture_region: Arabian Peninsula; Bedouin and town custom
13.meaning_for_kids: When someone visits, greet them warmly and offer them something before anything else.
13.saying: Arabic coffee is a sign of hospitality: guests are welcomed with 'Come in for coffee,' served coffee with dates, and refilled until they signal they have had enough.
13.source: Arabic coffee hospitality custom; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage 'Arabic coffee, a symbol of generosity' (2015)
13.reliability: Living custom, documented on Wikipedia citing UNESCO; details vary by region
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (door open to all)

13.value: A warm welcome for every guest
13.meaning_for_kids: When someone visits, we make them feel at home with a warm seat and something to eat.
13.saying: Under early Irish law a hospitaller (briugu) "had to have his house open to any guests"; the Triads name "three preparations of a good man's house: ale, a bath, a large fire."
13.original: briugu; Trí fuiric thige degduni: cuirm, fothrucud, tene mór. (Triad §97)
13.source: Brehon-law duty of hospitality of the briugu (public hospitaller), as summarised in Wikipedia 'Gaelic Ireland' and 'Early Irish law'; Triads of Ireland §97 (Meyer 1906)
13.reliability: Well-documented early Irish legal institution; triad wording from Meyer 1906
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (door open to all)

13.value: Caring about everyone, not just your own
13.meaning_for_kids: Be as kind to children from other families and groups as you are to your own.
13.saying: Mozi taught jian ai, 'inclusive care': care for every person equally, whatever their relationship to you, as you care for your own family.
13.reliability: Central Mohist doctrine (5th-4th c. BCE); summarized, not quoted
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (belonging, door open to all)

13.meaning_for_kids: When someone new arrives, offer a seat, a snack and a smile before asking lots of questions.
13.saying: Xenia, guest-friendship: hosts give a stranger a bath, food and safe passage, and wait until after the meal to ask who they are—as Nausicaa and Eumaeus do.
13.source: Homer, Odyssey Books 6–8 (Nausicaa and the Phaeacians) and Book 14 (the swineherd Eumaeus)
13.reliability: Well-documented ancient Greek custom; in Homer it is protected by Zeus, so keep stories secular
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (belonging, door open to all)

13.value: The whole world is one family
13.meaning_for_kids: Everyone, near or far, is part of one big family, so nobody is a stranger.
13.saying: 'This one is mine, that one is a stranger' - so count the small-minded. For the big-hearted, the whole earth is one family.
13.original: ayaṃ nijaḥ paro veti gaṇanā laghucetasām / udāracaritānāṃ tu vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (belonging, door open to all)

13.meaning_for_kids: When someone visits, give them a warm welcome, a good seat and something to share.
13.saying: Be one to whom a guest is as a god.
13.reliability: Canonical Upanishad (Hume translation cited on Wikipedia)
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (door open to all)

13.value: Warm bonds that grow through caring
13.meaning_for_kids: Doing small kind things together, day after day, makes people feel close like family.
13.saying: Jeong is the deep, warm bond between people: an 'invisible hug' shown through small acts of service and gift-giving that ties people together.
13.source: Korean cultural concept; described by David Tizzard, 'Korea in ten words: (5) Jeong', Korea Times, 14 July 2024
13.reliability: Widely discussed everyday cultural concept; no single classical source

13.value: A canoe that everyone may board
13.meaning_for_kids: Everyone is welcome to join in, and what is ours is shared with all.
13.saying: He waka eke noa – 'a canoe free for all to embark': a canoe shared by the whole community, so what belongs to one is available to all.
13.source: Te Aka Māori Dictionary, s.v. 'He waka eke noa' (listed as a whakataukī); Playcentre Aotearoa whakataukī sheet ('We are all in this together')
13.reliability: Te Aka entry with literal rendering and explanation; the sense 'we are all in this together' is also given by Playcentre.
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (belonging, door open to all)

13.meaning_for_kids: When someone arrives cold, hungry or tired, we first give them warmth, food and comfort.
13.saying: "Fire he needs who with frozen knees / Has come from the cold without; / Food and clothes must the farer have, / The man from the mountains come."
13.original: Elds er þörf, þeims inn er kominn ok á kné kalinn
13.source: Hávamál st. 3 (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1936 revised ed., text as on sacred-texts.com), stanza numbering per Bellows; same number in the Old Norse edition (Neckel / Guðni Jónsson)
13.reliability: Hávamál is in Codex Regius (c. 1270; poem older). Stanza number and Old Norse checked on heimskringla.no/wiki/Hávamál (Guðni Jónsson ed.); English checked word for word against Bellows on sacred-texts.com; quoted verbatim.
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (door open to all)

13.value: Together we find what we seek
13.meaning_for_kids: When we travel together and help each other, we find our group itself is the treasure.
13.saying: Led by the hoopoe, the birds cross seven valleys to find the Simorgh; only thirty arrive, and they find that they, 'si morgh' (thirty birds), are the Simorgh.
13.source: Farid ud-Din Attar, Manṭiq-uṭ-Ṭayr (The Conference of the Birds), 1177
13.reliability: Authentic Persian Sufi classic; widely translated (Darbandi & Davis 1984)

13.value: Welcoming the one who looks different
13.meaning_for_kids: We are kind to someone who looks different or is left out, and help them feel at home.
13.saying: Baby Zal, born with white hair, is abandoned on Mount Alborz; the great Simorgh bird carries him to her nest, raises him, and gives him a feather to call her in need.
13.source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (completed 1010), story of Zal and the Simorgh
13.reliability: Authentic Shahnameh episode (Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Zāl', cited on Wikipedia)
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (Belonging, door open to all)

13.meaning_for_kids: Making visitors feel at home by sharing your food, your space and a warm hello.
13.saying: Hoʻokipa is Hawaiian hospitality. Proverb: "Hoʻokahi nō lā o ka malihini" – a stranger only for a day.
13.original: Hoʻokahi nō lā o ka malihini
13.source: Pukui, ʻŌlelo Noʻeau (1983) (entry number not confirmed online), listed by Kamehameha Schools Aloha ʻĀina Project; hoʻokipa = hospitality: M. K. Tanaka, MA thesis, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (2017)
13.reliability: Widely recorded ʻŌlelo Noʻeau; Pukui entry number and full gloss not checked against the book
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (door open to all)

13.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
13.value: Room on the branch for everyone
13.meaning_for_kids: There is room for everyone to sit, whether big or small, so don't push anyone away.
13.saying: Let the kite perch and let the eagle perch; whoever says the other should not perch, let its wing break.
13.original: Egbe bere, ugo bere; nke sị ibe ya ebela, nku kwaa ya.
13.source: Igbo proverb (Nigeria), 'African Proverb of the Month' (Sept. 2026 entry by Elias Bushiri Élie), African Proverbs, Sayings and Stories, Tangaza University College, Nairobi (Igbo, English, Swahili and French wording)
13.reliability: Widely quoted Igbo proverb; Igbo text and English given on a university-hosted proverb archive, which reads it as: both birds have an equal right to the branch, enough room for everyone whatever their status. The 'wing break' ending is traditional curse-like wording; a picture book would use only the first half.
13.used_in_series: close to Book 13 (belonging, door open to all)

1.value: Courtesy, kindness and a friendly wave
1.meaning_for_kids: Smile, wave and say hello when you pass someone; being friendly makes everyone feel good.
1.saying: Torres Strait Islanders place a good deal of emphasis on courtesy and kindness. Always smile, wave and if within earshot, greet them with good morning, hello, or good night.
1.source: Torres Strait Regional Authority, 'TSRA Cultural Protocols Guide for TSRA Staff' (Feb 2011), 'Interpersonal Skills' p. 17 and 'Passing People' p. 13.
1.reliability: TSRA visitor guidance; both sentences verbatim from the PDF text, joined here. Page numbers approximate.

1.value: Never making anyone cry on purpose
1.meaning_for_kids: Try never to hurt someone's feelings on purpose, and help them if they are sad.
1.saying: 'I have made none to weep.' (one of the declarations of innocence)
1.source: Book of the Dead, spell 125 'declarations of innocence' (Papyrus of Ani, BM EA 10470); trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1898)
1.reliability: Primary funerary text; wording of the declarations varies from papyrus to papyrus

1.culture_region: Ancient Greece and Rome; Aesopic fables
1.meaning_for_kids: Asking gently and warmly works better than pushing, grabbing, or shouting.
1.saying: The blustering North Wind cannot tear off a traveller's cloak, but the Sun's gentle warmth makes him take it off. “Kindness effects more than severity.”
1.source: Aesop, The North Wind and the Sun (Perry Index 46; Avianus 4); moral as worded by J. Jacobs (1894)
1.reliability: Ancient Aesopic fable (Perry 46), known in classical Greece; Latin verse by Avianus

1.meaning_for_kids: Some people will be grumpy or selfish today; expect it and stay kind anyway.
1.saying: “Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial… I can neither be injured by any of them… for we are made for co-operation.”
1.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.1; trans. George Long (1862), Book Two, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
1.reliability: Primary Stoic text (c. AD 170-180); George Long's 1862 translation (public domain), wording confirmed on classics.mit.edu; section number follows standard numbering (Wikiquote); three clauses of the same paragraph joined with ellipses; the Greek is only the opening words, as printed on Wikiquote

1.value: Kindness is rewarded; envy is not
1.meaning_for_kids: Loving and caring for others brings good things; being jealous and mean doesn't.
1.saying: A kind old couple's beloved dog leads them to treasure and later helps the old man make bare cherry trees bloom; their envious neighbour copies them for gain and fails.
1.source: Japanese folktale ('The Old Man Who Made Flowers Bloom')
1.reliability: Traditional folktale; traditional versions include the dog's death, so soften for young children

1.value: Kindness to the weak, not greed
1.meaning_for_kids: Help hurt or small creatures because you care, not to win a prize.
1.saying: Kind Heungbu chased off a snake and mended a swallow's broken leg; its gift seed grew gourds full of treasure. Greedy Nolbu broke a swallow's leg himself, and his gourds brought disaster.
1.source: Heungbujeon, anonymous late-Joseon tale; pansori version Heungbo-ga (Bak-taryeong)
1.reliability: Classic folktale and novel (late Joseon); author unknown

1.meaning_for_kids: Making guests and friends feel welcome, safe and looked after.
1.saying: Manaakitanga: 'hospitality, kindness, generosity, support' – the process of showing respect, generosity and care for others.
1.source: Te Aka Māori Dictionary, s.v. manaakitanga; NZQA, Ngā Matapono programme guidance (Mana Tangata: 'reciprocity of kindness, respect, humanity')
1.reliability: Core Māori value; standard dictionary definition (Te Aka) and national qualifications guidance (NZQA).

1.value: A good deed comes back to you
1.meaning_for_kids: When we help others, they often remember and help us when we need it most.
1.saying: Ahiqar, wise chancellor to the Assyrian kings, is condemned after his nephew's lies; the executioner spares him because Ahiqar had once saved the executioner's own life.
1.source: Words (Story) of Ahiqar, narrative frame; Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine (5th c. BCE, TAD C1.1); later Syriac versions (Conybeare, Harris & Lewis 1913)
1.reliability: Ancient Aramaic text (Elephantine papyri), set at the courts of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon; Ahiqar is a literary sage

1.value: Compassion: feeling for others and helping
1.meaning_for_kids: Noticing when someone is sad or hurt and doing something kind to help.
1.saying: Wówauŋšila, 'compassion, kindness', is one of the Lakota virtues taught to children as shared by Lakota Elders.
1.source: Lakota virtues: WoLakota Project, 'Lakota Virtues' (South Dakota Office of Indian Education; teachings shared by Lakota Elders); Crazy Horse School, Wanblee (Oglala Sioux Tribe), mission/values page; M. Van Heuvelen (Cheyenne River Sioux), 'Lakota Values Endure', NMAI Smithsonian Voices (2020).
1.reliability: Lakota virtue on lists published by the SD Office of Indian Education (with Lakota Elders) and Crazy Horse School; spellings vary (Waounsila).

1.meaning_for_kids: Being gentle and kind with others, using soft hands and soft words.
1.saying: "Akahai", meaning kindness to be expressed with tenderness.
1.reliability: Official statute text; a modern legal codification of Native Hawaiian values

3.value: Working together for the good of all
3.meaning_for_kids: Everyone pitches in on a shared job, like tidying the playground, so the whole group benefits.
3.saying: Mink'a is unpaid communal work for the shared good: neighbours gather to build public works, clean irrigation canals, bring in harvests, or farm for elders and those who cannot.
3.source: Andean communal labour tradition from Inca times; Wikipedia 'Minka (communal work)' citing M.-E. Reeve, Los Quichua del Curaray (1988); listed among Andean reciprocity terms in Choque Quispe & Mamani Condori, 'Andean Traditions of Giving', ReVista (Harvard), 2002
3.reliability: Well-documented living practice (minga in Ecuador, faena in Peru)

3.culture_region: Four Quechua communities on the Apurímac River, southern Andes (Peru)
3.value: Everyone brings a rope to the bridge
3.meaning_for_kids: Every family adds its part, and together the job gets done and friends stay connected.
3.saying: Each year four Quechua communities rebuild a grass-rope bridge over the Apurímac: families twist thin cords that are braided into great ropes, a way to strengthen their bonds.
3.source: UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (2013): 'Knowledge, skills and rituals related to the annual renewal of the Q'eswachaka bridge'
3.reliability: UNESCO-inscribed living tradition (8.COM, 2013); includes rituals that should not be depicted

3.meaning_for_kids: Good friends help each other out of trouble, each in their own special way.
3.saying: Caught in a hunter's net, the ring-dove's flock flies off together; Zirak the mouse gnaws them free, and dove, crow, mouse, tortoise and gazelle become friends who keep saving one another.
3.source: Kalila wa Dimna, Arabic version by Ibn al-Muqaffa' (c. 750), chapter of the Ring-Dove
3.reliability: Classical text; Ibn al-Muqaffa's Arabic version of Indian/Persian fables (Panchatantra line)

3.meaning_for_kids: Big jobs and good things happen when we work together; nobody can do everything alone.
3.saying: One hand cannot clap.
3.source: Arabic proverb (also said يد واحدة لا تصفق); analysed in Tajudeen Yusuf, 'التعاون ركيزة للحياة: دراسة تحليلية للمثل العربي', Journal of Arabic Literature (Jali) 4:2, UIN Malang, 2023, which cites al-Hashimi, Jawahir al-Balagha (1999)
3.reliability: Widely used proverb; confirmed in a 2023 academic article; Maydani not checked

3.meaning_for_kids: Jobs that are too hard alone become possible when we work together.
3.saying: There is no strength without unity (literally, "no strength without putting together").
3.original: Ní neart go cur le chéile.
3.source: Irish proverb (seanfhocal): Ó Dónaill, Foclóir Gaeilge–Béarla (1977), on teanglann.ie, s.v. neart, sense 1(a), marked 'Prov.' (gloss 'unity is strength'); also on gleg.ie/gaeilge/seanfhocail/
3.reliability: Widely recorded Irish proverb; headword entry in Ó Dónaill with the gloss 'unity is strength'. Also in modern use as a slogan, which does not affect the traditional wording.

3.culture_region: Britain & United States; Masonic fraternity (18th-19th c.)
3.value: Spreading friendship that holds us together
3.meaning_for_kids: Kind acts are like glue between friends; they help a group stick together and work happily.
3.saying: The trowel is used "for the more noble and glorious purpose of spreading the cement of brotherly love and affection," so the only contest is who best can work and best agree.
3.source: Thomas Smith Webb, The Freemason's Monitor (1797; 1865 ed.), 'Remarks on the Third Degree', p. 78 (Master Mason working tools)
3.reliability: Published monitorial text (public domain); wording varies by jurisdiction

3.meaning_for_kids: Brothers, sisters and families who stick together are strong; quarrelling makes everyone weak.
3.saying: A father shows his quarrelling sons that single sticks snap easily but a tied bundle cannot be broken. “Union gives strength.”
3.source: Aesop, The Old Man and his Sons / The Bundle of Sticks (Perry Index 53; Babrius); moral as worded by J. Jacobs (1894)
3.reliability: Ancient Aesopic fable (Perry 53); Babrius' moral: brotherly love is the greatest good

3.value: Good for the swarm, good for the bee
3.meaning_for_kids: When everyone in your group does well, you do well too, so look after each other.
3.saying: “That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.”
3.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.54; trans. George Long (1862), Book Six, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
3.reliability: Primary Stoic text (c. AD 170-180); George Long's 1862 translation (public domain), wording confirmed on classics.mit.edu; section number follows standard numbering (Wikiquote) (the MIT page is unnumbered; 6.54 per Wikiquote's VI.54)

3.meaning_for_kids: A job too big for one can be easy when everyone works together.
3.saying: Trapped under a net, the doves' king says: 'At one moment and with one will, rising under the net, let us fly off with it.' A mouse friend then gnaws them free.
3.source: Hitopadesha Book 1 frame story (Arnold); also Panchatantra Book II frame
3.reliability: Classical Sanskrit fable; public-domain Arnold translation

3.meaning_for_kids: When we share our snack, we make friends, and together we can do hard things.
3.saying: On his journey Momotarō meets a dog, a monkey and a pheasant; each joins him in return for a share of his dumplings (kibi dango in modern versions), and together they succeed.
3.original: 桃太郎 · きびだんご
3.source: Japanese folktale; oldest surviving text the akahon 'Momotarō' (1723)
3.reliability: Traditional folktale; the quest involves fighting oni, so use only the sharing-and-teamwork thread

3.value: Many hands make a heavy job light
3.meaning_for_kids: A job that is heavy for one is easy for two, so ask for help and offer it.
3.saying: Even a sheet of paper is lighter when two people lift it together.
3.source: Traditional Korean proverb (속담); Hangul and literal sense as on the Indiana University Korean-program proverb list (korean.indiana.edu, item 16) and Clozemaster; also listed in Korean Wikipedia '속담'
3.reliability: Widely recorded proverb; Hangul confirmed in three sources

3.value: Staying close together, not far apart
3.meaning_for_kids: Stick with your friends instead of drifting apart or leaving someone out.
3.saying: Let us keep close together, not far apart.
3.original: Waiho i te toipoto, kaua i te toiroa
3.source: Te Aka Māori Dictionary, s.v. toipoto (example, citing Williams' dictionary, 1971); also s.v. kotahitanga ('unity, togetherness, solidarity, collective action'); Massey University whakataukī list; Playcentre Aotearoa sheet
3.reliability: Documented in Te Aka (with a dictionary citation) and on Massey and Playcentre lists; widely used for unity (kotahitanga). Its original context is not given in the sources opened.

3.value: Everyone joins in to finish the job
3.meaning_for_kids: Big jobs get done when everyone does their part.
3.saying: With red and black the work will be complete.
3.original: Mā whero, mā pango, ka oti ai te mahi
3.source: Te Papa, Matariki for teachers, 'What are our hopes and dreams for our community?' (lists the whakataukī as a community value; no English given); English gloss from the Playcentre Aotearoa whakataukī sheet
3.reliability: WEAKER: wording confirmed by Te Papa, but the English gloss comes only from Playcentre. The meaning (collective effort) and any iwi origin are unconfirmed; check with a cultural reader.

3.meaning_for_kids: Working with a partner, and accepting help from small friends, lets you solve big problems.
3.saying: The twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque face every trial together, even sending a mosquito ahead to find out which lords are real and which are wooden mannequins.
3.source: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya), Hero Twins in Xibalba; trans. D. Tedlock (1985/1996), A. Christenson
3.reliability: Popol Vuh, 16th-c. K'iche' text; foundational sacred narrative still important to many K'iche' today

3.meaning_for_kids: When friends each add a little help, together we can build something big.
3.saying: Hand added to hand, and a man's house is built up.
3.source: Sumerian Proverbs, Collection 2+6 (ETCSL 6.1.02), no. 2.138 (Segment B, ll. 14-15)
3.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian school tablets (c. 1800 BCE); the proverb's second half contrasts idle eating

3.value: Being brave together with a friend
3.meaning_for_kids: Scary things feel smaller when a friend stands beside us and we face them together.
3.saying: Look, Enkidu, two people together will not perish! A grappling-pole does not sink! No one can cut through a three-ply cloth!
3.source: Gilgamesh and Huwawa, version A (ETCSL 1.8.1.5), ll. 107-116
3.reliability: Primary text; Sumerian Gilgamesh poem, ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian copies

3.meaning_for_kids: One friend alone can give up, but friends who stick together can do hard things.
3.saying: A single arrow is weak and easily broken. A bundle of arrows tied together cannot be broken.
3.source: Haudenosaunee Peacemaker story; Smithsonian NMAI, Haudenosaunee Guide for Educators, p.3 (the Peacemaker breaks one arrow, then cannot break five tied together).
3.reliability: Traditional teaching within the Peacemaker story; wording as given in the Smithsonian NMAI educator guide.

3.meaning_for_kids: When everyone helps a little, even a big job becomes easy.
3.saying: Laulima ('many hands'). "ʻAʻohe hana nui ke alu ʻia." No task is too big when done together by all. (ʻŌlelo Noʻeau 142)
3.original: ʻAʻohe hana nui ke alu ʻia
3.source: Pukui, ʻŌlelo Noʻeau (1983), no. 142; laulima paired with this proverb in UH College of Education, Growing Pono Schools cards
3.reliability: Recorded proverb (Pukui 1983, #142); number confirmed in an Oregon Dept. of Education NHPI document

3.meaning_for_kids: A job too big for one is easy when everyone grabs a corner and helps.
3.saying: A bag of locusts is carried by holding it together. (Tshivenḓa: one finger cannot pick up grain.)
3.original: Kgetsi ya tsie e kgonwa ke go tshwaraganelwa (Setswana; printed in source as 'e kgona ke go tshwaragannwa'); Munwe muthihi a u ṱusi mathuthu (Tshivenḓa)
3.source: Setswana proverb, Gareegope, 'Aspect of Botho/Ubuntu in Botswana', University of Botswana Law Journal (June & Dec 2020), fn 40, p. 46 (glossed 'people should assist each other in life'); Tshivenḓa form in Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 6
3.reliability: Widely recorded proverb; spelling varies between sources

3.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
3.meaning_for_kids: Some jobs are too big to do alone, so ask friends to help and work together.
3.saying: One hand does not catch a buffalo.
3.source: Ewe proverb, No. 24 in Cephas Yao Agbemenu, Collection of 100 Ewe Proverbs (Nairobi: privately printed, Nov. 2010); 'African Proverb of the Month', Nov. 2010, African Proverbs, Sayings and Stories (Tangaza University College)
3.reliability: Ewe text and English printed by a named compiler on a university-hosted archive, which explains it as: isolated effort is weak, collective effort achieves much (the buffalo is among the most feared bush animals).

7.value: Don't steal, don't lie, don't be lazy
7.meaning_for_kids: Tell the truth, don't take what isn't yours, and do your share of the work.
7.saying: Ama qhilla, ama llulla, ama suwa: "don't be lazy, don't be a liar, don't be a thief." Bolivia's 2009 Constitution lists it among society's ethical principles.
7.original: Ama suwa, ama llulla, ama qhilla
7.source: Constitution of Bolivia (2009), Art. 8.I; formula first printed in the Memoirs of General Miller (London, 1829)
7.reliability: Popularly called the Inca moral code, but absent from colonial chronicles; earliest record 1829 (R. Cerrón Palomino; elbuho.pe fact-check). Present as a modern Quechua ethical saying, not an Inca law.

7.meaning_for_kids: A fib may seem to work for a moment, but the truth soon catches up, so tell the truth.
7.saying: The rope of lying is short.
7.source: Arabic proverb; English Wikiquote 'Arabic proverbs' cites Habib Ibrahim Katibah, The New Spirit in Arab Lands (1940), p. 121; English equivalent 'a lie has short legs'
7.reliability: Widely used proverb; one printed source (1940) cited on Wikiquote, no classical collection checked

7.value: Calm answers help the truth shine
7.meaning_for_kids: When we answer calmly and steadily, people can see that we are telling the truth.
7.saying: "Three doors through which truth is recognised: a patient answer, a firm pleading, appealing to witnesses."
7.original: Trí doruis a n-aichnither fír: frecra n-ainmnetach, ái fossad, sóud fri fíadnu.
7.source: The Triads of Ireland, ed. & tr. Kuno Meyer (Todd Lecture Series XIII, 1906), §174 (contrast §173, 'doors of falsehood: an angry pleading...')
7.reliability: Old Irish text, c. 850-900 CE; Meyer's translation (public domain)

7.value: It's okay to say 'I don't know'
7.meaning_for_kids: Say what you really know, and say 'I don't know' when you don't; that is being wise.
7.saying: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it; this is knowledge.
7.original: 知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也。
7.reliability: Canonical Analects text; Legge translation (1861, public domain)

7.value: Telling the truth and doing right
7.meaning_for_kids: Telling the truth and being fair keeps everything in balance, for you and for everyone.
7.saying: Ma'at was the Egyptian ideal of truth, balance, justice and right order; people aimed to live by it, declaring 'I have not uttered lies.'
7.source: Egyptian concept of Ma'at; declaration from Book of the Dead spell 125 (Papyrus of Ani), trans. Budge (1898)
7.reliability: Central, well-documented Egyptian concept (also personified as a goddess; keep stories secular)

7.culture_region: Britain & United States; Masonic fraternity (18th-19th c.)
7.meaning_for_kids: We say what really happened, even when it's hard, so others can trust us.
7.saying: "Truth is a Divine attribute, and the foundation of every virtue"; among Masons "hypocrisy and deceit are unknown."
7.source: Thomas Smith Webb, The Freemason's Monitor (1797; 1865 ed.), 'Remarks on the First Lecture', p. 41 (principal tenets: truth)
7.reliability: Published monitorial text (public domain); wording varies by jurisdiction

7.value: Telling the truth so people trust you
7.meaning_for_kids: If you trick people with fibs, they may not believe you when it really matters.
7.saying: A shepherd boy cries “Wolf!” as a joke; when a real wolf comes, nobody believes him. “A liar will not be believed, even when he speaks the truth.”
7.source: Aesop, The Shepherd Who Cried 'Wolf!' in Jest (Perry Index 210); moral as worded by J. Jacobs (1894)
7.reliability: Ancient Aesopic fable (Perry 210), recorded in Greek from classical times

7.meaning_for_kids: Telling the truth can feel scary, but the truth always wins out over a fib.
7.reliability: Canonical Upanishad; national motto of India

7.value: Doing right and telling the truth
7.meaning_for_kids: Telling the truth and doing the fair thing, even when nobody is watching.
7.saying: Tika means right, just and fair; pono means true, honest and sincere. Taught together with aroha (love, compassion) as three guiding values.
7.source: Te Aka Māori Dictionary, s.v. tika and pono; Te Kaharoa (AUT), 'Ko te Tika, ko te Pono, ko te Aroha: Exploring Māori values in the university'; Massey University whakataukī list ('Mā te tika, mā te pono, me te aroha')
7.reliability: Word senses confirmed in Te Aka; the tika-pono-aroha trio is treated as a set of core Māori values in the AUT article. Mead's Tikanga Māori was not opened; the child-level framing is editorial.

7.value: Fibs make the truth hard to believe
7.meaning_for_kids: If we fib, people may not believe us later, even when we are telling the truth.
7.saying: Tell a lie and then tell the truth: it will be considered a lie.
7.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian school tablets (c. 1800 BCE)

7.meaning_for_kids: Telling what really happened, even when it's hard, and not tricking yourself or others.
7.saying: Truth is to know all of these things. Speak the truth. Do not deceive yourself or others.
7.source: Seven Grandfather Teachings (Anishinaabe). Wording: Nogdawindamin Family & Community Services (Batchewana First Nation), 'The Seven Grandfather Teachings', nog.ca/who-we-are/about-nogdawindamin/seven-grandfathers-teachings. Ojibwe term & animal: GLIFWC, Maajii-Ojibwemowag language project, 'Amik & the Seven Grandfather Teachings'. Origin story: E. Benton-Banai, The Mishomis Book (1988).
7.reliability: Widely published by Anishinaabe organisations. Spellings and animal pairings vary by community; turtle for truth is the common pairing (GLIFWC; Georgian College citing Benton-Banai). Turtle for truth also confirmed by CBC Unreserved (2024).

7.value: Truth and doing what is right
7.meaning_for_kids: Telling the truth and doing the right thing keeps life in good order and makes us happy.
7.saying: Truth (asha) is the best good, and it is happiness: happiness to the one who is truthful for the sake of the best truth.
7.original: ašəm vohū vahištəm astī / uštā astī uštā ahmāi / hyat ašāi vahištāi ašəm
7.reliability: Authentic core Zoroastrian prayer; translations vary ('Order is the best good', Skjaervø; 'Truth is best', Humbach)

7.meaning_for_kids: What is true stays true, so telling the truth is always the right choice.
7.saying: "Truth is not changeable." (ʻŌlelo Noʻeau, Pukui 1983, p. 94)
7.source: Pukui, ʻŌlelo Noʻeau (1983), p. 94; cited in Duponte, Martin, Mokuau & Paglinawan, 'ʻIke Hawaiʻi – A Training Program for Working with Native Hawaiians', J. of Indigenous Voices in Social Work 1(1), 2010
7.reliability: Recorded proverb; English and page confirmed, but the online copy of the Hawaiian line is garbled – check spelling and entry number in Pukui

7.value: Cheating is never just a game
7.meaning_for_kids: A little trick or fib isn't harmless fun; it can grow into a habit, so stay truthful.
7.saying: Dishonesty is not a game; it should not be made a habit.
7.original: Boferefere ga se papadi, ga bo a tshwanelwa go itlwaetswa
7.source: Setswana saying, Gareegope, 'Aspect of Botho/Ubuntu in Botswana', University of Botswana Law Journal (June & Dec 2020), fn 40, p. 46 (glossed 'lack of honesty is not an admirable trait')
7.reliability: Recorded Setswana saying; one academic source, English is a close rendering

7.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
7.value: What you take wrongly, you can't enjoy
7.meaning_for_kids: If you take something that isn't yours, you can't enjoy it out in the open.
7.saying: The thief that stole the king's trumpet, where would he play it?
7.original: Ole ti o gbe kakaki oba, ibo ni o ti fon?
7.source: Yorùbá proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, pp. 6-7
7.reliability: Recorded Yorùbá proverb (printed without tone marks); the article lists it without a separate gloss, meaning given is the plain sense

8.value: Carrying a message carefully, passing it on
8.meaning_for_kids: When someone trusts you with a message or a job, you do it carefully and pass it on exactly.
8.saying: Inca relay runners carried messages between road stations; each runner repeated the message until the next had it perfectly, so nothing was lost.
8.source: Guamán Poma de Ayala, Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (1615); Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609); T. N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002) — via Wikipedia 'Chasqui'
8.reliability: Historical institution recorded by colonial chroniclers and archaeologists

8.value: Keeping safe what others trust you with
8.meaning_for_kids: If a friend asks you to look after something, keep it safe and give it back.
8.saying: Al-Samaw'al (d. c. 560) guarded armour left in his care and would not hand it over even under siege; Arabs say 'more faithful than al-Samaw'al.'
8.source: Classical proverb 'awfa min al-Samaw'al'; story of Imru' al-Qais's armour in classical Arabic lore
8.reliability: Widely recorded classical proverb; the full story includes a violent siege, so retell only the promise-keeping

8.value: Keep your promises; they are worth gold
8.meaning_for_kids: When you say 'I will,' do it, so friends can always count on you.
8.saying: A saying of Chu: getting a hundred jin of gold is not as good as getting one promise from Ji Bu, a man who always kept his word.
8.source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) ch. 100, Biography of Ji Bu and Luan Bu; idiom 一諾千金
8.reliability: Historical anecdote recorded by Sima Qian (c. 90s BCE); the four-character idiom is a later condensation

8.meaning_for_kids: When someone trusts you to pass on a message, say it just the way they said it.
8.saying: If you are a man of entry sent by official to official... carry out the mission for him as he says.
8.source: Maxims of Ptahhotep, maxim 8 (Lichtheim numbering, AEL I, 1973); P. Prisse 7,3-5; UCL Digital Egypt translation
8.reliability: Primary text; Middle Kingdom copy (P. Prisse, BnF), set in the Old Kingdom

8.culture_region: Ancient Greece and Rome; Aesopic fables
8.value: True friends stay when it's scary
8.meaning_for_kids: A real friend stays and helps you when something scary happens.
8.saying: When a bear appears, one traveller climbs a tree and leaves his friend alone. Afterwards the friend says: “Never trust a friend who deserts you at a pinch.”
8.source: Aesop, The Travellers and the Bear (Perry Index 65; Avianus); moral as worded by J. Jacobs (1894)
8.reliability: Ancient Aesopic fable (Perry 65), first in Latin verse by Avianus

8.value: Keeping a promise and repaying kindness
8.meaning_for_kids: When we promise something, we keep it, even when we're very curious.
8.saying: A man saves a wounded crane; a woman comes to live with him and weaves wondrous cloth, asking him never to look. He peeks, sees the crane, and she must leave.
8.source: Japanese folktale ('The Crane's Return of a Favour'); many regional variants

8.value: Being true and trustworthy with friends
8.meaning_for_kids: Keep your word to friends and tell them the truth, so they can trust you.
8.saying: Third of the five secular precepts: 'Trust among friends': keep your friendships with faithfulness and sincerity.
8.source: Samguk sagi vol. 45, Biography of Gwisan: the 'five precepts for secular life' (sesok ogye) given by the monk Won'gwang (c. 600) to Gwisan and Chwihang
8.reliability: Recorded in Samguk sagi (1145); traditionally presented as the Hwarang ethos

8.meaning_for_kids: When we promise a friend something we keep it, because broken promises break trust.
8.saying: The eagle and the serpent swear to be friends and share food with their young; the eagle breaks the oath, eats the serpent's children, and ends up trapped in a pit.
8.source: Myth of Etana (Old Babylonian, Middle Assyrian and Nineveh versions), eagle-and-serpent episode; trans. S. Dalley, Myths from Mesopotamia (2000), pp. 189ff.
8.reliability: Authentic Akkadian tale known from several versions; summary per Wikipedia citing Dalley

8.meaning_for_kids: We only promise what's true, and then we do what we promised.
8.saying: Second counsel: swear no oath unless you know it is true; bitter is the fate of one who breaks his word.
8.original: Þat ræð ek þér annat, at þú eið né sverir, nema þann er saðr sé; grimmar limar ganga at tryggðrofi; armr er vára vargr
8.source: Sigrdrífumál st. 23, the second numbered counsel (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: own close rendering of Bellows st. 23 ('Then second I rede thee, to swear no oath / If true thou knowest it not; / Bitter the fate of the breaker of troth'), Bellows 1936 ed. on sacred-texts.com; same number in the Old Norse edition
8.reliability: Stanza number, Old Norse (heimskringla.no) and Bellows wording checked (earlier draft's 'harsh bonds' replaced by the Bellows sense, 'bitter the fate of the troth-breaker'). Bellows' note: the counsels in st. 22-37 resemble Loddfáfnismál and probably did not originally belong to this speech.

8.meaning_for_kids: When we say 'I promise' we really do it, so friends can always count on us.
8.saying: Mithra, whose name means 'covenant' or 'contract', is the ever-watchful guardian of promises in the Avesta's Mihr Yasht; breaking one's word brings disaster.
8.reliability: Authentic Avestan hymn; summary per Encyclopaedia Iranica (Hintze, Kellens) as cited on Wikipedia

8.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
8.meaning_for_kids: When you learn to do things well and kindly, you're trusted with bigger things.
8.saying: If a child knows how to wash his hands clean, he will dine with elders: wisdom, not age, earns a place.
8.original: Ti omode ba mon owo we a ba agba jeun
8.source: Yorùbá proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 11
8.reliability: Recorded Yorùbá proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal (printed without tone marks)

8.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
8.culture_region: Mande / Malinke (Mali, Guinea); Manden Charter, c. 1236
8.value: Never betray a friend; keep your word
8.meaning_for_kids: Do what you said you'd do, and never turn against someone who trusts you.
8.saying: Never betray one another. Respect your word of honour.
8.source: Manden Charter (Kouroukan Fouga), Article 23, English text translated from French, 'Kouroukan Fouga - Indigenous Constitution of Ancient Mali' (ccaf.africa); the Charter is inscribed by UNESCO as 'the Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga' (2009, decision 4.COM 13.59)
8.reliability: Oral charter attributed to c. 1236; a French version was published in 1998 and this English text is a translation from French, so wording and numbering vary slightly between versions. UNESCO calls it one of the oldest constitutions in the world, albeit mainly oral.

20.value: Doing your work with care, to the end
20.meaning_for_kids: Take care with each step of a job, and finish it so it's ready to use.
20.saying: Itqan: mastery, doing a piece of work carefully and thoroughly all the way to the finish, as craftspeople weave palm-leaf baskets strand by strand.
20.source: Arabic craft ideal itqan (root t-q-n, 'to master, perfect'); A² Book 20 back-matter note
20.reliability: Standard Arabic word; its best-known praise is a saying attributed to the Prophet (keep that for the Hadith category); here only the secular craft sense

20.value: Doing your very best to the end
20.meaning_for_kids: We give a job our full effort and keep going until it is finished.
20.saying: Ganbaru means "to commit oneself fully to a task and to bring that task to an end": to keep going through tough times.
20.source: Everyday Japanese verb and value; e.g. the slogan 'Gambarō Kobe' after the 1995 earthquake

20.value: Taking pride in doing work well
20.meaning_for_kids: We do our jobs carefully and well, because our good work helps others.
20.saying: A shokunin has "a social obligation to work his best for the general welfare of the people": skill joined with pride and care.
20.source: Japanese artisan ethic; Toshio Odate, Japanese Woodworking Tools: Their Tradition, Spirit and Use (1984)
20.reliability: Quoted from a published craftsman's book; widely cited concept

20.meaning_for_kids: If you build or do something slowly and carefully, it will be strong and last.
20.saying: Would a tower built with devoted effort ever collapse?
20.source: Traditional Korean proverb (속담); wording and sense as given in Wikipedia 'Korean proverbs'

20.value: Finish the work to make it valuable
20.meaning_for_kids: A pile of good beads is only a necklace once you thread them all; finish what you start.
20.saying: Even three bushels of beads become a treasure only when they are strung.
20.source: Traditional Korean proverb (속담); Hangul and English gloss as on the Indiana University Korean-program proverb list (korean.indiana.edu, item 19)
20.reliability: Widely used proverb, but confirmed in only one source I opened (a course page); double-check against a Korean dictionary

20.value: Doing your craft with skill and care
20.meaning_for_kids: Make things carefully and well—your drawing, your block tower, your tidy room.
20.saying: Tōltēcayōtl, ‘Toltec-ness’, means the art of living; a toltecatl was a skilled craftsperson—the ideal of doing things with wisdom, skill and care.
20.source: Alonso de Molina, Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana (1571); M. León-Portilla, Toltecáyotl
20.reliability: Molina's dictionary entries verified; the 'art of living' framing is León-Portilla's modern interpretation

20.meaning_for_kids: Before a big job: think about it, make a plan, do it, then check how it went.
20.saying: Diné College's philosophy follows Sa'ah Naagháíí Bik'eh Hózhóón through four steps: Nitsáhákees (thinking), Nahat'á (planning), Iiná (living) and Siihasin (assuring).
20.source: Diné College, 'Educational Philosophy' (dinecollege.edu), based on Sa'ah Naagháíí Bik'eh Hózhóón, 'the Diné traditional living system'.
20.reliability: Published by Diné College, the Navajo Nation's tribal college; spellings as on the college site. Rooted in a sacred framework.
20.used_in_series: close to Book 20 (Doing it well and finishing)

20.meaning_for_kids: Keep going on a hard job until it's finished, even when your arms feel tired.
20.saying: "E kaupē aku nō i ka hoe a kō mai." Keep paddling: go on with what you started and finish it. (ʻŌlelo Noʻeau 319)
20.original: E kaupē aku nō i ka hoe a kō mai
20.reliability: Recorded proverb (Pukui 1983, #319); listed with number and meaning by Kamehameha Schools

20.meaning_for_kids: Try your very best and climb a little higher every day.
20.saying: "Kūlia i ka nuʻu." Strive to reach the highest. (ʻŌlelo Noʻeau 1913)
20.reliability: Recorded proverb (Pukui 1983, #1913); number confirmed in UH Mānoa compilation

20.value: Small steady steps finish big jobs
20.meaning_for_kids: Even if you're slow, little steps, one after another, will get the whole job done.
20.saying: The dog can finish water with its tongue: even the slowest worker finishes the task.
20.source: isiZulu proverb, Masuku & Chiliza, 'Cross-parallels in isiZulu proverbial messages', South African Journal of African Languages 41(1), 2021, 69-75, doi:10.1080/02572117.2021.1902140, p. 71
20.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal
20.used_in_series: close to Book 20 (finishing what you start)
