14.meaning_for_kids: Before hurting anyone, think: how would I feel if that happened to me?
14.saying: A lioness grieving her lost cubs is reminded that the animals she hunted had families too; feeling their pain, she gives up eating meat.
14.source: Kalila wa Dimna, Arabic version by Ibn al-Muqaffa' (c. 750), chapter of the Lioness
14.reliability: Classical fable; the loss of the cubs is central, so handle gently

14.meaning_for_kids: People need each other, like animals huddling together under one big tree in the rain.
14.saying: People live in one another's shelter.
14.original: Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine.
14.source: Irish proverb (seanfhocal): Ó Dónaill, Foclóir Gaeilge–Béarla (1977), on teanglann.ie, s.v. scáth, marked 'Prov.' (the dictionary prints the dialect form 'a mhaireas'); modern form 'a mhaireann' on gleg.ie/gaeilge/seanfhocail/ (Gaillimh le Gaeilge)
14.reliability: Widely recorded Irish proverb; headword entry in Ó Dónaill (gloss 'man is a social animal'). English is a literal rendering: scáth = shade, shadow, shelter.

14.meaning_for_kids: That worried feeling when someone is about to get hurt is kindness; follow it and help.
14.saying: Anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity. The feeling of commiseration is the beginning of humanity.
14.original: 今人乍見孺子將入於井，皆有怵惕惻隱之心。
14.reliability: Canonical Mencius text (4th c. BCE); famous 'four sprouts' passage

14.value: Treat others how you want to be treated
14.meaning_for_kids: If something would hurt you, don't do it to someone else.
14.saying: One should never do to another what one regards as hurtful to oneself. This, in brief, is the rule of right conduct.
14.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva 113.8 (Brihaspati's teaching, Ganguli numbering)
14.reliability: Canonical epic; chapter confirmed, verse number per Ganguli edition

14.meaning_for_kids: Look at faces and listen closely to notice when a friend is sad, tired or needs space.
14.saying: Nunchi, literally 'eye-measure', is the quiet skill of listening and gauging other people's moods so you can respond kindly.
14.source: Korean cultural concept; first recorded in the 17th c. (National Institute of Korean Language), as cited in Wikipedia 'Nunchi'

14.culture_region: Sasanian and early Islamic-era Iran; Zoroastrian Middle Persian texts
14.value: Treat others as you want treating
14.meaning_for_kids: If we wouldn't like something done to us, we don't do it to others.
14.saying: Whatever is disagreeable to yourself do not do unto others.
14.reliability: Authentic Middle Persian Zoroastrian texts (9th-c. compilations of older teaching); listed in Wikipedia 'Golden Rule'

14.value: Feeling others' pain as our own
14.meaning_for_kids: When a friend hurts we feel it too and want to help, because we are all one family.
14.saying: The children of Adam are members of one body, created from one essence. When time brings pain to one limb, the other limbs cannot rest.
14.original: بنى آدم اعضای یک پیکرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند (banī-ādam aʿzā-ye yek peykarand / ke dar āfarīnesh ze yek gowharand)
14.source: Saadi, Gulistan (1258), ch. 1 'On the Conduct of Kings', story 10 ('Bani Adam')
14.reliability: Authentic; one of the most famous Persian poems (UN carpet, 2005). First line has two manuscript readings (yek peykar / yekdigar)

14.value: Becoming yourself through caring for others
14.meaning_for_kids: We become our best selves by caring for others and letting others care for us.
14.saying: A person is a person through other people.
14.original: Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu (isiZulu); Motho ke motho ka batho (Sesotho/Setswana); Munhu munhu nevanhu (Shona)
14.source: Ubuntu/Botho maxim; Samkange & Samkange, Hunhuism or Ubuntuism (1980); Univ. of the Free State PUO glossary 'Ubuntu'; Gareegope, 'Aspect of Botho/Ubuntu in Botswana', University of Botswana Law Journal (June & Dec 2020), p. 46
14.reliability: Widely recorded maxim; confirmed in university and journal sources (Sesotho also 'ka batho ba bang')
14.used_in_series: Book 14 The View From Down Low

14.value: Truly seeing and greeting each other
14.meaning_for_kids: Saying hello and really noticing someone tells them, 'I see you, and you matter.'
14.saying: The everyday isiZulu greeting 'Sawubona' literally means 'we see you'; the usual reply 'Ngikhona' means 'I am here' (used as 'I am well').
14.source: isiZulu everyday greeting; Unisa 'Learn online Zulu', Theme 1 (Sawubona = hello; Ngikhona = I am well); Wiktionary 'sawubona' (contraction of siyakubona, 'we see you')
14.reliability: Genuine everyday greeting; literal meanings are linguistic. The 'I see your soul' reading and the reply 'Shiboka' come from 1990s Western management books: don't present those as tradition
14.used_in_series: close to Book 14 (empathy; greeting quoted in its note)

14.meaning_for_kids: Big and small friends spot different things, so everyone's eyes and ideas are needed.
14.saying: The vultures have not seen you, the ant has seen you: what the high flyer misses, the small one on the ground notices.
14.source: isiZulu proverb, Masuku & Chiliza, 'Cross-parallels in isiZulu proverbial messages', South African Journal of African Languages 41(1), 2021, 69-75, doi:10.1080/02572117.2021.1902140, p. 73
14.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal
14.used_in_series: close to Book 14 (seeing from a small friend's view)

6.value: Staying calm and gentle when provoked
6.meaning_for_kids: When someone makes you cross, take a slow breath and answer gently instead of exploding.
6.saying: Hilm (forbearance, calm self-mastery) was prized in old Arab ethics as the mark of a wise, civilised person; its opposite, jahl, meant hot-headed, reckless behaviour.
6.source: Classical Arab ethical concept, as analysed by Goldziher and Izutsu
6.reliability: Well-established concept in scholarship on early Arab ethics

6.value: Don't take your anger out on others
6.meaning_for_kids: If you feel cross about one thing, don't snap at someone who didn't cause it.
6.saying: He did not transfer his anger; he did not repeat a fault.
6.source: Analects 6.3 (Yong Ye; Legge VI.2), praise of the disciple Yan Hui
6.reliability: Canonical Analects text; Legge translation (1861, public domain)

6.meaning_for_kids: Calm friends grow strong like trees in a sunny field; stomping and shouting helps no one.
6.saying: The heated man is 'like a tree growing indoors'; the truly silent man is 'like a tree grown in a meadow' that grows green and gives fruit and shade.
6.source: Instruction of Amenemope, ch. 4 (Lichtheim, AEL II, 1976; COS 1.47); P. BM EA 10474
6.reliability: Primary text; New Kingdom (Ramesside), well-preserved papyrus BM EA 10474

6.culture_region: Britain & United States; Masonic fraternity (18th-19th c.)
6.meaning_for_kids: Feelings like anger are okay, but we keep them inside a safe circle so nobody gets hurt.
6.saying: The compass "teaches us to limit our desires in every station"; Masons are taught to "keep their passions within due bounds."
6.source: Thomas Smith Webb, The Freemason's Monitor (1797; 1865 ed.), 'Remarks on the First Lecture' (furniture of the Lodge: the compasses)
6.reliability: Published monitorial text; many US rituals say 'circumscribe our desires and keep our passions within due bounds'; wording varies by jurisdiction

6.meaning_for_kids: When anger feels big, stop, breathe, and then choose what to do.
6.source: Delphic maxims, Sosiades' list in Stobaeus, Anthology (Wachsmuth–Hense vol. 3, pp. 125–128), no. 16
6.reliability: Sosiades' list preserved by Stobaeus (5th c. AD); many maxims match a 4th–3rd c. BC stele from Miletopolis; Delphic origin is traditional

6.meaning_for_kids: When we shout mean things in anger, the hurt comes back to us too.
6.saying: You should not curse strongly: it rebounds on you.
6.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian copies

6.meaning_for_kids: When anger or worry clouds your thinking, you can clear it and choose kind actions.
6.saying: The opposite of good mind isn't a bad or evil mind. It's what we call a clouded mind.
6.source: Good Mind, part of the Peacemaker's message of 'peace, power and the Good Mind' (NYSED Indigenous Education unit 'The Great Law of Peace'). Quote: Michael Martin (Onondaga, Beaver Clan; Native American Community Services), WNED/Buffalo Toronto Public Media 'Heritage Moments', 9 Nov 2021.
6.reliability: Quote from a named Onondaga speaker in public media; concept widely taught by Haudenosaunee educators. Rooted in the Creation Story and Great Law, so treat as spiritual.

6.value: Real strength is staying calm when angry
6.meaning_for_kids: Being truly strong means staying calm and kind even when we feel angry.
6.saying: They that with raging elephants make war / Are not, so deem the wise, the truly brave; / But in real verity, the valiant are / Those who, when angered, are not passion's slave.
6.source: Saadi, Gulistan (1258), tale of Harun al-Rashid and his angry son; 19th-c. English verse rendering
6.reliability: Authentic Gulistan verse; English rendering as quoted in Wikipedia's Gulistan article (translator and chapter number not confirmed online; usually printed in ch. 1)

6.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
6.value: A soft word turns anger back
6.meaning_for_kids: A gentle, friendly answer can calm an angry friend faster than shouting back.
6.saying: A soft word causes anger to turn back.
6.source: Igbo proverb, F. C. Ogbalu, Ilu Igbo: The Book of Igbo Proverbs (Onitsha: Varsity Press, 1965), 'Kindness and Wickedness' no. 7; English draft translation by Frances W. Pritchett (franpritchett.com), glossed there 'Humble words soften anger'
6.reliability: Entry in a published 1965 Igbo proverb collection; the English is a draft translation and the Igbo text is not shown on the web page, so 'original' is left blank. Meaning matches 'gentle answer' proverbs found in many cultures.

15.value: Finding your way when things go wrong
15.meaning_for_kids: When plans fall apart, stay calm, look for a way, and keep going until you get home.
15.saying: On each of seven voyages Sinbad is shipwrecked or trapped, yet each time he finds a way out and makes it home to Baghdad.
15.source: Sinbad the Sailor tales, attached to One Thousand and One Nights (manuscripts from the 17th c.; core tales older)
15.reliability: Folk story cycle; added to the Nights late, core tales possibly 9th-14th century

15.value: Lift yourself up; be your own friend
15.meaning_for_kids: When you fall or feel down, you can cheer yourself on and get back up.
15.saying: Lift yourself up by yourself; do not let yourself sink. You alone are your own friend, and you alone can be your own enemy.

15.value: Getting back up every time you fall
15.meaning_for_kids: When you fall or fail, you get up and try again, one more time than you fell.
15.saying: Fall down seven times, get up eight.
15.original: 七転び八起き (nana korobi ya oki)
15.source: Japanese proverb (kotowaza); linked with the self-righting Daruma doll

15.value: Keep finding ways until it works
15.meaning_for_kids: If one way doesn't work, try another until you get through.
15.saying: A problem is solved by continuing to find solutions.
15.original: I orea te tuatara ka puta ki waho
15.source: Massey University, 'Whakataukī – Māori proverbs' (Inspiring whakataukī); same saying, with a variant ending ('ka patu ki waho'), on the Playcentre Aotearoa whakataukī sheet
15.reliability: Gloss from Massey. The two lists spell the ending differently (ka puta / ka patu ki waho) and cite no classical source; have a cultural reader confirm the wording and the literal image.

15.meaning_for_kids: Staying calm and strong, and not giving up when something is hard or takes long.
15.saying: Wówačhiŋtȟaŋka, glossed 'patience, self-control' (WoLakota) and 'perseverance' (NMAI), 'continues to guide the decisions of Lakota leaders today.'
15.source: Lakota virtues: WoLakota Project, 'Lakota Virtues' (South Dakota Office of Indian Education; teachings shared by Lakota Elders); Crazy Horse School, Wanblee (Oglala Sioux Tribe), mission/values page; M. Van Heuvelen (Cheyenne River Sioux), 'Lakota Values Endure', NMAI Smithsonian Voices (2020).
15.reliability: Lakota virtue; English glosses vary between patience, fortitude and perseverance across Lakota sources.

15.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
15.value: Sticking with it through hard times
15.meaning_for_kids: Good things often come after hard work and tough days, so don't give up.
15.saying: Whoever would prosper would endure hardship.
15.original: Oju eni ti o ma la, a ri iyonu
15.source: Yorùbá proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 14
15.reliability: Recorded Yorùbá proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal (printed without tone marks)

15.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
15.value: Standing up when others doubt you
15.meaning_for_kids: When people laugh or say you can't, you can still keep trying until you stand on your own feet.
15.saying: In the Mande epic of Sunjata (Sundiata), the future king is slow to walk (still unable at seven) and is mocked, until he suddenly stands and walks with the aid of an iron bar.
15.source: Sunjata/Sundiata, Mande oral epic of Mali told by griots (jeli); childhood episode as summarised in Ronica Roth, 'Mali's Boy-King: A Thirteenth-Century African Epic Becomes Digital', Humanities (NEH) 19(4), July/Aug 1998; cross-checked with Wikipedia 'Epic of Sundiata', which cites D. T. Niane (1960)
15.reliability: Oral epic with many versions: in some the iron rod breaks and he rises using a baobab branch, so the exact detail varies, but the standing-up-after-mockery episode is consistent. The wider epic includes warfare and sorcery, which the seed leaves out.

4.value: Saying sorry, even when it's hard
4.meaning_for_kids: When you've been unkind, go and say sorry properly; it can make you friends again.
4.saying: Jealous general Lian Po learned that Lin Xiangru avoided quarrels to protect their kingdom. Ashamed, he carried thorny brambles on his bare back to Lin's door and begged forgiveness; they became firm friends.
4.source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) ch. 81, Biographies of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru
4.reliability: Historical anecdote recorded by Sima Qian (c. 90s BCE); idiom in everyday use

4.meaning_for_kids: When someone has said sorry, don't keep bringing it up; start fresh together.
4.saying: Po-i and Shu-ch'i did not keep the former wickednesses of men in mind, and hence the resentments directed towards them were few.
4.original: 伯夷叔齊不念舊惡，怨是用希。
4.reliability: Canonical Analects text; Legge translation (1861, public domain)

4.meaning_for_kids: If a friend owes you something and is having a hard time, be kind and let most of it go.
4.saying: If you find a large debt against a poor man, make it into three parts; forgive two, let one stand.
4.source: Instruction of Amenemope, ch. 13 (Lichtheim, AEL II, 1976; COS 1.47); P. BM EA 10474
4.reliability: Primary text; New Kingdom (Ramesside), well-preserved papyrus BM EA 10474

4.meaning_for_kids: After a fight, find a way to make up and be friends again.
4.source: Delphic maxims, Sosiades' list in Stobaeus, Anthology (Wachsmuth–Hense vol. 3, pp. 125–128), no. 112
4.reliability: Sosiades' list preserved by Stobaeus (5th c. AD); many maxims match a 4th–3rd c. BC stele from Miletopolis; Delphic origin is traditional

4.value: Don't pay back meanness with meanness
4.meaning_for_kids: When someone is unkind, the best answer is to stay kind instead of copying them.
4.saying: “The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrongdoer.”
4.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.6; trans. George Long (1862), Book Six, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
4.reliability: Primary Stoic text (c. AD 170-180); George Long's 1862 translation (public domain), wording confirmed on classics.mit.edu; section number follows standard numbering (Wikiquote)

4.value: Saying sorry to everyone, starting fresh
4.meaning_for_kids: Once a year, say sorry for any hurt you caused, and forgive others too.
4.saying: At the end of Paryushana, Jains ask one another: 'Micchami dukkadam' - if I have hurt you in any way, knowingly or unknowingly, please forgive me.
4.source: Samvatsari (last day of Paryushana) forgiveness practice; formula from the Jain pratikramana rite

4.value: Friendship can grow stronger after a quarrel
4.meaning_for_kids: After a fight or a hard time, friends who talk and make up can end up closer than before.
4.saying: After rain, the ground becomes firm.
4.original: 雨降って地固まる (ame futte ji katamaru)
4.source: Japanese proverb (kotowaza); Digital Daijisen, Nihon Kokugo Daijiten and Kotowaza o shiru jiten, via Kotobank; earliest cited example Yoshiwara suzume (1667)
4.reliability: Widely recorded proverb; in use since the 16th-17th century; the dictionary also lists a Korean parallel

4.meaning_for_kids: After a fight, we say sorry and come back together as friends.
4.saying: Hohou rongo means 'to make peace'; the verb hohou also means 'to bind together, lash together'.
4.source: Te Aka Māori Dictionary, s.v. hohou and hohou rongo; New Zealand Law Society, LawTalk 954, 'Kia hohou te rongo: restoring balance through dispute resolution'
4.reliability: Dictionary definition (Te Aka). The Law Society article describes hohou te rongo as a Māori-values approach to resolving disputes that can include karakia and spiritual guidance, so keep the story at the everyday 'making up' level.

4.meaning_for_kids: If someone is mean to us, we can choose to be kind back and help make peace.
4.saying: Do not return evil to the man who disputes with you; requite with kindness your evil-doer ... smile on your adversary.
4.source: Counsels of Wisdom (Babylonian, Akkadian), passage on returning good for evil; ed. W. G. Lambert, Babylonian Wisdom Literature (1960), pp. 96-107
4.reliability: Authentic Babylonian wisdom text (Lambert's edition); English wording as quoted by Nolland (2005), cited on Wikipedia; exact line numbers not checked online

4.meaning_for_kids: After a fight, we can put away hurtful things and start again as friends.
4.saying: They uprooted a white pine tree and threw their weapons into the hole. They replanted the tree on top of the weapons and named it the Tree of Peace.
4.source: Haudenosaunee Peacemaker story (Great Law of Peace); Smithsonian NMAI, Haudenosaunee Guide for Educators, p.3 'Peacemaker Story'.
4.reliability: Foundational Haudenosaunee oral history, as retold in the Smithsonian NMAI educator guide; also the origin of 'burying the hatchet'.

4.value: Not paying back hurts in the family
4.meaning_for_kids: When a brother or sister hurts us, we try to make peace instead of hitting back.
4.saying: First counsel: be blameless toward your kin, and seek no revenge even when they wrong you.
4.original: Þat ræð ek þér it fyrsta, at þú við frændr þína vammalaust verir; síðr þú hefnir, þótt þeir sakar geri
4.source: Sigrdrífumál st. 22, the first of the numbered counsels (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: own close rendering of Bellows st. 22 ('Then first I rede thee, that free of guilt / Toward kinsmen ever thou art; / No vengeance have, though they work thee harm'), Bellows 1936 ed. on sacred-texts.com; same number in the Old Norse edition
4.reliability: Stanza number, Old Norse (heimskringla.no) and Bellows wording checked. Bellows' note: the counsels in st. 22-37 resemble Loddfáfnismál and probably did not originally belong to this speech; Codex Regius breaks off at the first line of st. 29, the later counsels come from paper copies.

4.value: Setting things right in the family
4.meaning_for_kids: When there is a hurt, the family sits together, talks it out, says sorry, forgives and lets it go.
4.saying: Hoʻoponopono, 'setting to right': a family gathering, led by a respected elder, where everyone talks through a hurt, says sorry, forgives (kala) and releases it.
4.source: Pukui, Haertig & Lee, Nānā I Ke Kumu, Vol. 1 (Queen Liliʻuokalani Children's Center / Hui Hānai, 1972), section on hoʻoponopono; Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary (1986), s.v. hoʻoponopono
4.reliability: Traditional family practice documented by Pukui (1972); NOT the modern New-Age 'I'm sorry, please forgive me' prayer, which is excluded

4.value: Not giving up on someone over one fault
4.meaning_for_kids: When someone you love makes a mistake, help them fix it, and keep loving them.
4.saying: You do not disown your child because it has scabies: a small flaw is no reason to break a bond.
4.original: A u laṱi ṅwana nga phaḓi
4.source: Tshivenḓa proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 9
4.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal

4.value: Owning it when you hurt someone
4.meaning_for_kids: If you hurt someone, they remember it, so notice, own up and say sorry.
4.saying: The offended never forgets; the offender does.
4.source: isiZulu proverb, Masuku & Chiliza, 'Cross-parallels in isiZulu proverbial messages', South African Journal of African Languages 41(1), 2021, 69-75, doi:10.1080/02572117.2021.1902140, p. 72
4.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal

4.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
4.meaning_for_kids: Even when you misbehave, your family still loves you and helps you do better.
4.saying: A child cannot be so unruly that we feed it to a lion: faults are corrected, but the bond is kept.
4.original: Omo eni ki buru ka fi fun ekun pa je
4.source: Yorùbá proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 9
4.reliability: Recorded Yorùbá proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal (printed without tone marks); 'ekun' usually means leopard, the article renders 'lion'

5.value: Knowing you have enough is being rich
5.meaning_for_kids: Feeling happy with the toys, snacks and friends you already have is a kind of treasure.
5.saying: He who is satisfied with his lot is rich.
5.reliability: Received Daodejing text (attrib. Laozi); Legge translation (1891, public domain)

5.value: Being happy with what you have
5.meaning_for_kids: A simple snack with a happy heart beats a pile of stuff with grumbles.
5.saying: Better is bread with a happy heart than wealth with vexation.
5.source: Instruction of Amenemope, ch. 6 (Lichtheim, AEL II, 1976; COS 1.47); P. BM EA 10474
5.reliability: Primary text; New Kingdom (Ramesside), well-preserved papyrus BM EA 10474

5.meaning_for_kids: Notice the kind things people do for you, and say thank you.
5.source: Delphic maxims, Sosiades' list in Stobaeus, Anthology (Wachsmuth–Hense vol. 3, pp. 125–128), no. 106
5.reliability: Sosiades' list preserved by Stobaeus (5th c. AD); many maxims match a 4th–3rd c. BC stele from Miletopolis; Delphic origin is traditional

5.value: Remembering help given in hard times
5.meaning_for_kids: A small kindness when you really needed it is a giant gift - always remember it.
5.saying: Help given in the moment of need, though small, is greater than the whole world.
5.original: kālattiṉāṟ ceyta naṉṟi ciṟiteṉiṉum / ñālattiṉ māṇap peritu
5.reliability: Canonical Tamil classic (dated c. 300 BCE-500 CE, debated); kural number, chapter and Tamil text confirmed on thirukkural.net

5.value: Thanking everyone who made our meal
5.meaning_for_kids: Before eating we thank the farmers, cooks and nature that gave us our food.
5.saying: Meals begin with itadakimasu ("I humbly receive"), thanking everyone and everything that made the food possible, and end with gochisōsama deshita.
5.original: いただきます · ごちそうさまでした

5.meaning_for_kids: When someone helps you, remember it and find a way to help them back.
5.saying: A traveller saved a bird's chicks from a snake; later the grateful birds came to his rescue. The legend gives Chiaksan ('Pheasant Peak') its name.
5.source: Folk legend of Chiaksan, Wonju (Gangwon Province); retold for children as 'The Grateful Magpie'
5.reliability: Local legend with many versions (pheasant in the Chiaksan legend, magpie in children's retellings); only the rescue-from-snake core and the place-name link were checked online (double-check); traditional ending involves a temple bell (omit)

5.culture_region: Aotearoa New Zealand; Māori New Year
5.meaning_for_kids: At new year we remember loved ones, say thanks for what we have, and hope.
5.saying: Matariki's three guiding principles: remembrance, celebrating the present (gathering to give thanks for what we have), and looking to the future (the promise of a New Year).
5.source: Matariki Advisory Group, 'Values for Matariki celebrations' (MBIE); includes the saying 'Matariki hunga nui' (Matariki gathers people together)
5.reliability: Official advisory-group report to government; principles paraphrased from it. The star cluster has spiritual and iwi-specific meanings that vary by region.

5.value: Remembering who made and cares for you
5.meaning_for_kids: Remember and say thank you to the people who look after you.
5.saying: In the creation story the wooden people “had no soul and soon lost loyalty” to those who had made them, and so they did not last.
5.source: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya), creation of humans: mud, then wood, then maize; trans. A. Christenson
5.reliability: Popol Vuh, 16th-c. K'iche' text; foundational sacred narrative still important to many K'iche' today; wording via Wikipedia 'Mesoamerican creation myths'

5.meaning_for_kids: Say 'tlazohcamati' to thank anyone who helped you, big or small.
5.saying: Tlazocamati: “to be thankful; to thank someone for something” (Molina, 1571). Karttunen records the spelling tlazohcamati as the Nahuatl expression of thanks.
5.source: Online Nahuatl Dictionary (Wired Humanities Projects, Univ. of Oregon), entry 'tlazocamati', citing A. de Molina, Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana (1571), part 2, f. 118r, and F. Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl (1992), p. 306
5.reliability: Dictionary entry citing Molina (1571) and Karttunen (1992), read on the Online Nahuatl Dictionary; the entry gives no etymology, so none is claimed here

5.value: Not getting too upset over lost things
5.meaning_for_kids: Finding something is fun, and losing something is okay; we can still feel happy inside.
5.saying: I have found it -- a cause for celebration! I have lost it -- my heart does not ache!
5.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian school tablets (c. 1800 BCE); reading it as contentment is an interpretation

5.value: Enjoying simple everyday joys with family
5.meaning_for_kids: Good food, a warm bath, clean clothes and holding hands with family are everyday treasures.
5.saying: Let your belly be full ... Make merry each day ... Let your clothes be clean ... Gaze on the child who holds your hand, let a wife enjoy your repeated embrace!
5.source: Epic of Gilgamesh, Old Babylonian version, 'Sippar' tablet (Meissner fragment, VA+BM), col. iii, ll. 6-13, the alewife's advice; trans. A. R. George, The Epic of Gilgamesh (Penguin, 2000), pp. 123-5; ed. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (OUP, 2003), pls. 17-19, discussion pp. 275-279
5.reliability: Authentic Old Babylonian passage (18th c. BCE, probably from Sippar). Wording follows George's translation as reproduced by ETANA (Vanderbilt), lines selected with ellipses. The OB tablet calls the speaker 'the alewife'; the name Siduri appears only in the later Standard Babylonian version. George reads the advice as accepting one's allotted lot, not plain hedonism.

5.value: Giving thanks to the natural world first
5.meaning_for_kids: Saying thank you to water, plants, animals, sun and each other before starting the day.
5.saying: Gatherings open by greeting and thanking each part of the natural world — waters, plants, animals, winds, sun, moon and stars — each section ending 'Now our minds are one.'
5.original: Ohén:ton Karihwatéhkwen (Mohawk: 'the words that come before all else')
5.source: Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address. Six Nations Indian Museum & The Tracking Project, 'Thanksgiving Address: Greetings to the Natural World' (1993; Mohawk by Rokwaho, English by John Stokes & Kanawahienton), reprinted NMAI Smithsonian Voices (22 Nov 2018); NMAI Haudenosaunee Guide for Educators p.11; Akwesasne children's recitation, NFB/Ocean School.
5.reliability: Traditional Haudenosaunee address, said at the start and end of gatherings; wording varies by speaker and nation. Published version authorised by the Six Nations Indian Museum.

5.value: Everyone has something to be glad about
5.meaning_for_kids: Even on hard days, there is always something good in our lives to be thankful for.
5.saying: "All wretched is no man, though never so sick; / Some from their sons have joy, / Some win it from kinsmen, and some from their wealth, / And some from worthy works."
5.original: Erat maðr alls vesall, þótt hann sé illa heill
5.source: Hávamál st. 69 (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1936 revised ed., text as on sacred-texts.com), stanza numbering per Bellows; same number in the Old Norse edition (Neckel / Guðni Jónsson)
5.reliability: Hávamál is in Codex Regius (c. 1270; poem older). Stanza number and Old Norse checked on heimskringla.no/wiki/Hávamál (Guðni Jónsson ed.); English checked word for word against Bellows on sacred-texts.com; quoted verbatim (earlier draft had 'kin' for Bellows' 'kinsmen'; corrected).

5.value: Being happy with what you have
5.meaning_for_kids: Being happy with what we already have feels better than always wanting more.
5.saying: If you desire power, desire nothing but contentment, which is its own kingdom.
5.source: Saadi, Gulistan (1258), ch. 2 'On the Morals of Dervishes', story 28 (Rehatsek/Newman translation)
5.reliability: Authentic; translations vary (Gladwin: 'seek only for contentment which is inestimable wealth')

5.value: Remembering and thanking those who helped you
5.meaning_for_kids: Remember the friends who helped you, thank them, and be kind to them in return.
5.saying: 'The one who was helped has now turned against his helpers': a warning never to forget those who helped you.
5.original: Nyavhumbwa wa dagaila, wa kanda vho u vhumbaho
5.source: Tshivenḓa proverb, Sebola & Abodunrin, 'Indigenised Critical Thinking and Epistemic Cognitions: An Ethnopragmatic Analysis of Tshivenḓa and Yorùbá Proverbs', Southern African Journal for Folklore Studies 31(2), 2021, doi:10.25159/2663-6697/9446, p. 13
5.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal

5.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
5.value: Noticing what is always there for you
5.meaning_for_kids: Notice and thank the people and things that are always there for you, like family, food and water.
5.saying: A fish is in water but does not know the importance of water.
5.original: Akpa le tome gake menya tsi fe vevie nyenyeo.
5.source: Ewe proverb, No. 25 in Cephas Yao Agbemenu, Collection of 100 Ewe Proverbs (Nairobi; listed in 2009 as a forthcoming booklet); 'African Proverb of the Month', Oct. 2009, African Proverbs, Sayings and Stories (Tangaza University College)
5.reliability: Ewe text and English printed by a named Ewe-proverb compiler (Kenyatta University, Fine Arts) on a university-hosted archive, which explains it as 'taking things for granted'. The entry's own example is about a powerful person's family; the gratitude angle for children is my reading.

19.value: Learning, sticking at it, being teachable
19.meaning_for_kids: Anyone can grow wise by learning, keeping at it, and being willing to be taught.
19.saying: "Three things that make a fool wise: learning, steadiness, docility."
19.original: Tréde immifoilnge gáis do báeth: ecna, fosta, sochoisce.
19.source: The Triads of Ireland, ed. & tr. Kuno Meyer (Todd Lecture Series XIII, 1906), §194
19.reliability: Old Irish text, c. 850-900 CE; Meyer's translation (public domain)

19.value: Everyone around you can teach you something
19.meaning_for_kids: Friends, grown-ups, even little ones can show you something new: copy the good, skip the bad.
19.saying: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
19.original: 三人行，必有我師焉。擇其善者而從之，其不善者而改之。
19.reliability: Canonical Analects text; Legge translation (1861, public domain)

19.value: Asking others instead of showing off
19.meaning_for_kids: Even when you know a lot, ask others and listen; everyone can teach you something.
19.saying: Do not be proud on account of your knowledge... discuss with the ignorant as with the wise.
19.source: Maxims of Ptahhotep, maxim 1 (Lichtheim numbering, AEL I, 1973); P. Prisse 5,8-10; UCL Digital Egypt translation
19.reliability: Primary text; Middle Kingdom copy (P. Prisse, BnF), set in the Old Kingdom
19.used_in_series: Book 19 The Beetle Who Knew the Stars

19.value: Good ideas can come from anyone
19.meaning_for_kids: The quietest or smallest friend may have the best idea, so listen to everyone.
19.saying: Fine words are more sought after than greenstone, but can be found with the women at the grindstone.
19.source: Maxims of Ptahhotep, maxim 1 (Lichtheim numbering, AEL I, 1973); P. Prisse 5,8-10; UCL Digital Egypt translation
19.reliability: Primary text; Middle Kingdom copy (P. Prisse, BnF), set in the Old Kingdom

19.meaning_for_kids: It's smart to say 'I don't know yet' and then ask or find out.
19.saying: Socrates says he is wiser in one small way: “what I do not know I do not think I know either.”
19.original: ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι
19.reliability: Primary text (Plato). The popular 'I know that I know nothing' is a later paraphrase, not found verbatim in Plato

19.value: Others may see what you can't
19.meaning_for_kids: Your friend may be seeing another side of the same thing, so listen before you argue.
19.saying: Truth has many sides. In the parable, blind men each touch one part of an elephant - trunk, leg, tusk - and each is only partly right.
19.original: anekāntavāda; andha-gaja-nyāya (maxim of the blind men and the elephant)
19.source: Jain doctrine of anekantavada; parable used in Jain texts (e.g. Mallisena, Syadvadamanjari, 13th c.)
19.reliability: Core Jain doctrine; parable also in Buddhist Udana 6.4

19.culture_region: Japan; Zen tradition, popularised in the US
19.meaning_for_kids: Even when we know a lot, we stay curious and ready to learn new ways.
19.saying: In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities, but in the expert's mind there are few.
19.source: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (1970), Prologue
19.reliability: Verified published quotation (1970); concept from Zen Buddhism

19.value: The more you know, the humbler you are
19.meaning_for_kids: The ripest rice bows its head; people who are really good at something don't brag.
19.saying: The riper the rice, the lower its head hangs.
19.original: 実るほど頭を垂れる稲穂かな (minoru hodo kobe o tareru inaho kana)
19.source: Japanese proverb (kotowaza); Kotowaza o shiru jiten and Digital Daijisen, via Kotobank; dictionary traces it to a haikai verse in Kefukigusa (1638) contrasting ripening rice with proud people
19.reliability: Widely recorded proverb; the 1638 source verse is older than the current 5-7-5 wording

19.value: Not boasting about your own good
19.meaning_for_kids: You don't need to brag about what you're good at; others will notice.
19.saying: The kūmara does not speak of its own sweetness.
19.original: Kāore te kūmara e kōrero mō tōna ake reka
19.source: Playcentre Aotearoa whakataukī sheet (wording and English); Tāhūrangi (Ministry of Education), 'Kūmara Reka' resource, which gives the variant 'E kore te kūmara e kōrero mō tana reka' and asks why the kūmara does not talk about how good he is
19.reliability: Widely used; wording varies between sources (Kāore/E kore; tōna ake/tana). Humility is the commonly given meaning, but the sources opened give no classical citation.

19.value: Not bragging, so people trust you
19.meaning_for_kids: If we don't show off or brag, friends believe us when we tell them something important.
19.saying: You should not boast; then your words will be trusted.
19.reliability: Primary text; ETCSL (Oxford) translation of Old Babylonian copies

19.value: Knowing you are equal, not better
19.meaning_for_kids: Nobody is better than anybody else; we each have a place, and we need each other.
19.saying: Humility is to know yourself as a sacred part of Creation. You are equal to others, but you are not better.
19.source: Seven Grandfather Teachings (Anishinaabe). Wording: Nogdawindamin Family & Community Services (Batchewana First Nation), 'The Seven Grandfather Teachings', nog.ca/who-we-are/about-nogdawindamin/seven-grandfathers-teachings. Ojibwe term & animal: GLIFWC, Maajii-Ojibwemowag language project, 'Amik & the Seven Grandfather Teachings'. Origin story: E. Benton-Banai, The Mishomis Book (1988).
19.reliability: Widely published by Anishinaabe organisations. Spellings and animal pairings vary by community; wolf for humility is the common pairing (GLIFWC; Georgian College citing Benton-Banai). Nogdawindamin notes the word can also mean 'compassion'.

19.meaning_for_kids: We let others finish talking before we speak, instead of cutting in to show off.
19.saying: Whoever interrupts other people's conversation to show off his own wisdom only shows how little he knows.
19.source: Saadi, Gulistan (1258), ch. 8 'Rules for Conduct in Life', maxim 82 (numbering varies by translation)
19.used_in_series: close to Book 19 (asking instead of telling, humility)

19.value: Everyone sees only part of the picture
19.meaning_for_kids: Each of us knows only a piece, so we listen to others and put our pieces together.
19.saying: In a dark room, people touch an elephant and call it a water spout, a fan, a pillar, a throne; if each had a candle, their differences would disappear.
19.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book III, 'The Elephant in the Dark' (Arberry, Tales from the Masnavi, no. 71); earlier version in Sanai's Hadiqa
19.reliability: Authentic Masnavi tale (Arberry translation), unlike the many fake 'Rumi quotes' online; book number from standard editions

19.meaning_for_kids: Doing your best without bragging, and letting others shine too.
19.saying: "Haahaa", meaning humility, to be expressed with modesty.
19.reliability: Official statute text; a modern legal codification of Native Hawaiian values

19.value: A humble heart, open to learning
19.meaning_for_kids: Being humble enough to say "teach me", and happy to learn from others.
19.saying: Anga fakatōkilalo / loto tō, 'humility, open to learning', is one of the four pillars of Tongan society.
19.source: Tongan Working Group, 'Fofola e fala kae talanoa e kāinga: A Tongan conceptual framework' (NZ Ministry of Social Development, 2012), pp. 12–14
19.reliability: Published Tongan community framework (NZ MSD); the four pillars are attributed to Queen Sālote's 1964 speech

19.tradition: West Africa (Akan, Yoruba, Igbo, Mali & neighbours)
19.value: No one holds all the wisdom
19.meaning_for_kids: Even a very small child can teach you something you missed, so listen to everyone.
19.saying: Kwaku Ananse gathers all the world's knowledge into a gourd to hang in a tree; his small son shows him how to climb, Ananse sees he missed something, and the gourd bursts, sharing wisdom with all.
19.source: R. S. Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1930), Tale 3, 'How wisdom came among the tribe' (the Ananse and the pot of wisdom tale)
19.reliability: Collected Ashanti tale (Rattray, 1930), widely retold as 'Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom'; plot confirmed from the archive.org text of Rattray. Retellings vary (pot or gourd, who gives the advice). In Rattray, Ananse belongs to the Sky-god's 'spider stories'; the seed drops that frame.

9.value: Doing the right thing takes courage
9.meaning_for_kids: If you know what's right, like helping or telling the truth, be brave and actually do it.
9.saying: To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage.
9.reliability: Canonical Analects text; Legge translation (1861, public domain)

9.value: Speaking up for what's fair, again and again
9.meaning_for_kids: If something unfair happens, keep asking clearly and politely for it to be put right.
9.saying: A peasant robbed of his donkeys by a bully pleads for justice before the high steward nine times, ever more eloquently, until his goods are returned.
9.source: The Eloquent Peasant, Middle Kingdom (c. 1850 BCE); Lichtheim, AEL I (1973); Parkinson (1991, 1997)
9.reliability: Primary literary text preserved on several Middle Kingdom papyri

9.value: Being brave in a scary new place
9.meaning_for_kids: When you feel scared and alone, take a breath, calm your heart, and be brave.
9.saying: Stranded on an island, the sailor is told not to fear: 'If you are brave and control your heart, you will embrace your children... you will see your home.'
9.source: Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor, P. Hermitage (Leningrad) 1115, Middle Kingdom; after Lichtheim, AEL I (1973)
9.reliability: Primary literary text; Wikipedia confirms the advice to be brave and control his heart, wording after Lichtheim

9.culture_region: Britain & United States; Masonic fraternity (18th-19th c.)
9.value: Staying steady when things are scary
9.meaning_for_kids: Being brave means holding steady and keeping going, even when we feel afraid.
9.saying: Fortitude is "that noble and steady purpose of the mind whereby we are enabled to undergo any pain, peril, or danger."
9.source: Thomas Smith Webb, The Freemason's Monitor (1797; 1865 ed.), 'Remarks on the First Lecture', p. 43 (the four cardinal virtues)
9.reliability: Published monitorial text (public domain); wording varies by jurisdiction

9.meaning_for_kids: Being brave isn't doing wild things or never trying; it's the careful middle.
9.saying: Courage is the middle way between two mistakes: too little daring is cowardice, too much is rashness.
9.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6–7 (1106a–1107b), the doctrine of the mean
9.reliability: Primary text; standard reading of Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness)

9.value: Doing it is easier than worrying
9.meaning_for_kids: Something scary often turns out easier once we try it than while we worry.
9.saying: Giving birth is easier than worrying about it: trying is usually easier than we fear.
9.original: 案ずるより産むが易し (anzuru yori umu ga yasushi)

9.meaning_for_kids: Even if you're the smallest, you can be brave and use your clever ideas.
9.saying: A boy only one inch tall sails to the capital in a rice bowl, with a chopstick oar and a needle for a sword, and bravely drives off an ogre.
9.source: Japanese folktale; Muromachi-period otogizōshi version, softened in Meiji retellings by Iwaya Sazanami
9.reliability: Traditional tale; the old otogizōshi version includes trickery, so use the common modern version

9.meaning_for_kids: Keep going bravely and don't give up when things feel hard.
9.saying: Be strong, be brave, be steadfast.
9.original: Kia kaha, kia māia, kia manawanui
9.source: Widely used Māori exhortation and school motto; word senses from Te Aka Māori Dictionary (manawanui: 'steadfast, resolute, patient, persistent'; māia: 'brave'); English rendering as on Kuraplan, 'A Whakataukī to Remember'
9.reliability: WEAKER: very widely used motto, but none of the sources opened traces it to a classical whakataukī collection. Each word is confirmed in Te Aka. Treat as a modern saying unless a cultural reader confirms an origin.

9.value: Doing what is right, even when scary
9.meaning_for_kids: Being brave means doing the right thing even when you feel scared or nervous.
9.saying: Aakode'ewin means 'state of having a fearless heart': to face the foe with integrity, and to do what is right even when the consequences are unpleasant.
9.source: Seven Grandfather Teachings (Anishinaabe). Wording: Nogdawindamin Family & Community Services (Batchewana First Nation), 'The Seven Grandfather Teachings', nog.ca/who-we-are/about-nogdawindamin/seven-grandfathers-teachings. Ojibwe term & animal: GLIFWC, Maajii-Ojibwemowag language project, 'Amik & the Seven Grandfather Teachings'. Origin story: E. Benton-Banai, The Mishomis Book (1988).
9.reliability: Widely published by Anishinaabe organisations. Spellings and animal pairings vary by community; bear for bravery is the common pairing (GLIFWC; Georgian College citing Benton-Banai). Bear = a mother protecting her young (Algonquins of Pikwakanagan; Georgian College).
9.used_in_series: close to Book 09 (Courage, finding your voice)

9.meaning_for_kids: Brave, kind-hearted people don't let fear rule them, so they feel happier.
9.saying: "The lives of the brave and noble are best, / Sorrows they seldom feed; / But the coward fear of all things feels, / And not gladly the niggard gives."
9.original: Mildir, fræknir menn bazt lifa, sjaldan sút ala
9.source: Hávamál st. 48 (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1936 revised ed., text as on sacred-texts.com), stanza numbering per Bellows; same number in the Old Norse edition (Neckel / Guðni Jónsson)
9.reliability: Hávamál is in Codex Regius (c. 1270; poem older). Stanza number and Old Norse checked on heimskringla.no/wiki/Hávamál (Guðni Jónsson ed.); English checked word for word against Bellows on sacred-texts.com; quoted verbatim (full stanza).

9.meaning_for_kids: When someone is being unfair, we can bravely speak up and ask friends to help.
9.saying: Kaveh the blacksmith rises against the cruel king Zahhak; he raises his leather apron on a spear as a banner, and the people gather behind him.
9.source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (completed 1010), story of Zahhak and Kaveh
9.reliability: Authentic Shahnameh episode; Kaveh is a legendary figure, often invoked in modern politics
9.used_in_series: close to Book 09 (Courage, finding your voice)

9.value: Staying steady when things get stormy
9.meaning_for_kids: When something is scary, a brave friend stays calm and helps steer everyone through.
9.saying: "He hoʻokele waʻa no ka lā ʻino." A steersman for a stormy day – said of a courageous person. (ʻŌlelo Noʻeau 592)
9.original: He hoʻokele waʻa no ka lā ʻino
9.reliability: Recorded proverb (Pukui 1983, #592); listed with number and meaning by Kamehameha Schools

9.meaning_for_kids: Feeling scared is normal; being brave means trying anyway, one step at a time.
9.saying: Fear is nothing; victory is courage.
9.source: isiZulu proverb, Masuku & Chiliza, 'Cross-parallels in isiZulu proverbial messages', South African Journal of African Languages 41(1), 2021, 69-75, doi:10.1080/02572117.2021.1902140, p. 73
9.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal

12.value: Telling your story helps after hard times
12.meaning_for_kids: After something scary or sad, talking about it with someone kind helps you feel better.
12.saying: To comfort the frightened sailor, the island's great serpent shares its own sad story: 'How happy is he who tells what he has tasted, when the bad time has passed.'
12.source: Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor, P. Hermitage (Leningrad) 1115, Middle Kingdom; after Lichtheim, AEL I (1973)
12.reliability: Primary literary text; the serpent telling its story is confirmed online, the quoted line is after Lichtheim (please double-check)

12.value: Telling a friend what's on your heart
12.meaning_for_kids: Keeping worries inside hurts; sharing our feelings with a trusted friend makes them lighter.
12.saying: "Be never the first to break with thy friend / The bond that holds you both; / Care eats the heart if thou canst not speak / To another all thy thought."
12.original: vin þínum ver þú aldregi fyrri at flaumslitum; sorg etr hjarta, ef þú segja né náir einhverjum allan hug
12.source: Hávamál st. 121 (Poetic Edda, Codex Regius c. 1270); English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1936 revised ed., text as on sacred-texts.com), stanza numbering per Bellows (Loddfáfnismál; lines 4-7 of Bellows' seven-line stanza); same number in the Old Norse edition (Neckel / Guðni Jónsson)
12.reliability: Hávamál is in Codex Regius (c. 1270; poem older). Stanza number and Old Norse checked on heimskringla.no/wiki/Hávamál (Guðni Jónsson ed.); English checked word for word against Bellows on sacred-texts.com; quoted verbatim.
12.used_in_series: close to Book 12 (sharing feelings with someone safe)

12.value: Speaking up when you need help
12.meaning_for_kids: If something is wrong, tell a grown-up you trust; nobody can help if they don't know.
12.saying: A child who does not cry dies on the mother's back: if you never say what is wrong, no one can help.
12.source: isiZulu proverb, Masuku & Chiliza, 'Cross-parallels in isiZulu proverbial messages', South African Journal of African Languages 41(1), 2021, 69-75, doi:10.1080/02572117.2021.1902140, pp. 71-72
12.reliability: Recorded proverb with translation in a peer-reviewed journal; the literal wording is stark, so use the meaning, not the words, with children
12.used_in_series: close to Book 12 (sharing feelings with someone safe)

11.value: Kindness comes back around to you
11.meaning_for_kids: When you are kind to someone, it helps them and, sooner or later, kindness comes back to you.
11.saying: Kindness to others is not only for their sake: it goes around and comes back to you.
11.original: 情けは人の為ならず (nasake wa hito no tame narazu)
11.source: Japanese proverb (kotowaza); Digital Daijisen (Shogakukan) and Kotowaza o shiru jiten, via Kotobank; Daijisen cites the Agency for Cultural Affairs usage survey (2022)
11.reliability: Widely recorded proverb; often misread as 'kindness does others no good' (the 2022 survey was split about evenly); the dictionary meaning is used here; one dictionary links it to Buddhist cause-and-effect
11.used_in_series: close to Book 11 (kindness grows when shared)

11.meaning_for_kids: When you are kind to others, kindness finds its way back to you.
11.saying: If kindness is sown, then kindness you shall receive.
11.original: He aroha whakatō, he aroha puta mai
11.source: Massey University, 'Whakataukī – Māori proverbs' (Māori Language Week whakataukī list); same wording and gloss on the Playcentre Aotearoa whakataukī sheet
11.reliability: Widely used whakataukī; gloss as given by Massey and Playcentre. Neither opened source cites a classical collection, so the origin is unconfirmed.
11.used_in_series: close to Book 11 (kindness grows when shared)
